events.summary: Curated by Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK School and Lisa Jarrett Drawing from the Museum’s collection, this exhibition is co-curated by Lisa Jarrett, an artist, educator, and curator, and the Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK Elementary— a group of 4th and 5th grade curators from KSMoCA. Working from a conversation with notable curators Dr. Lowery Stokes Sims and Dr. Leslie King Hammond, the exhibition engages PAM’s collection in new dialogues shaped by emerging curatorial voices and multigenerational knowledge. From theme and concept development, through work selection, and installation, this community curators project highlights the collaborative nature of curatorial practice and museum work. Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK School \(HTC\) is a KSMoCA project. Students participate directly in shaping exhibitions, positioning them as contributors to the museum, and engaging them as researchers, writers, planners, and curators. Through workshops and field trips, students collaborate with artists, visiting curators, and mentors from Portland State University’s College of the Arts. They research how exhibitions are developed, how artworks are interpreted, and how institutional decisions shape public understanding. Expanded curatorial practice includes visual art, writing, performance, research, publishing, and social practice. Co-founded by Lisa Jarrett and Harrell Fletcher, the project began in 2018 at Harriet Tubman Middle School and continues in its current iteration at Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Elementary School.
events.title: Harriet Tubman Center Museum

events.summary: Inspired by Katherine Ace’s 9 Portraits as the foundational starting point for the exhibition, Nine Women Artists will feature the work of the artists shown in Ace’s portrait painting. All mature artists in their careers and with a significant presence in the Northwest, their work reveals a diverse expression of artistic styles from representation to abstraction. There are rich details in the painting. Most notably on the left hangs Henri Fantin-Latour’s A Studio at Les Batignolles, 1870 \(Musée d’Orsay\). In this painting is a formal gathering of male artists. In response to this painting, Katherine asked her subjects to dress in their studio/work clothes as counterpoint, all marked in their characteristic poses. Other Portland women artists are recognized here through their paintings—a small Sally Haley still life hangs in the background, as well as an Amanda Snyder painting behind Phyllis Yes. And to the far right, we have a glimpse of Lucinda Parker’s very large work. Postcards and newspapers scattered on the floor are the exhibition announcements and reviews highlighting the artists’ works. An epic portrait featuring nine women artists of the Northwest, Ace responded to the lack of self-portraits by women artists in history. From left, the artists are: Laura Ross-Paul, Katherine’s self-portrait seated with phone, Mary Josephson, Judy Cooke, Phyllis Yes, Sharon Bronzan, Shu-Ju Wang, Lucinda Parker, and Sherrie Wolf. All are women artists who have made long careers in Portland. As Ace notes about these women, “They have tenacity, have lived through sexist decades, told they couldn’t really be artists—only fit for sleeping with the professor, expected to subvert themselves to male artist machismo.”
events.title: Nine Women Artists

events.summary: Dashing dachshunds, endless sausages, polka, pilsner, pretzels and more will take over Oaks Park Sept. 25-27 during the park’s ever-popular Oktoberfest. The three-day, family-friendly celebration of autumn will be packed with traditional food and beverages, authentic music and dancing and an array of Oktoberfest activities for revelers of all ages. “Over the years, Oaks Park’s Oktoberfest has grown into one of our most popular celebrations of the year,” said Emily MacKay, Oaks Park’s Marketing and Events Director. “From great food and drinks to live music, Bavarian cooking shows, wiener dog races and even a pretzel toss contest, we have something for everyone.” Oaks Park has been hosting its Oktoberfest since the early 1990s. This year’s festival will feature all the favorites that have made the festival at Oaks Park so popular, including: Food and drink: A range of imported Paulaner beers will be available along with craft ciders and wines. Food vendors include Schnitzel Haus, Brat Barn, Wienerwurst, Eis Hutte, the Buffalo Gap and others. Activities: The three-day fest will feature an all-ages dance floor, Bavarian cooking shows, wiener dog races, a pretzel toss, a condiment art contest, a vendor village, a Chicken Dance contest and more. There will also be the kid-friendly Kinderplatz on Saturday and Sunday, where kids can find fun arts, crafts and music. Music: It’s not Oktoberfest without great polka, and Oaks Park has a full lineup, from The Polkatones and The Tirolean Dancers to The Alpine Echoes and accordionist Elizabeth Wisler. In addition to all the Oktoberfest fun, Oaks Park will have its rides, games and other attractions running at full speed. Gate-only admission for Oktoberfest is $7.50 for those 48” and taller and $4.50 for those under 48”. Gate admission with a Ride Bracelet is $44.45 for guests 48” and taller and $23.45 for anyone under 48”. Infants 2 and under are free. Oaks Park’s classic roller-skating rink and mini golf course will also be available for guests for an additional price. Hours for Oktoberfest at Oaks Park are: 4 p.m. to 10 p.m. Friday, Sept. 25; 11 a.m. to 10 p.m. Saturday, Sept. 26; and 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. Sunday, Sept. 27. Video highlights of last year’s Oktoberfest can be seen here. For more information about this year’s Oktoberfest at Oaks Park, including schedules, activity details and more, visit Oakspark.com.
events.title: Portland's favorite Oktoberfest returns to Oaks Park Sept. 25-27

events.summary: More than 40 leading local architecture firms present the best designs they hoped to build but that didn’t come to pass. Projects will include Allied Works’ elegant proposal commissioned by the New York Metropolitan Museum for its Modern and Contemporary Art Wing, West of West’s concept studies for infill housing in Los Angeles and Portland, Henneberry Eddy’s adaptive reuse of the recently destroyed Centennial Mills, and many more. In addition, the exhibition offers visions from Portland’s past, from Edward Bennett’s 1932 plan to reenvision Portland in the City Beautiful movement to Skidmore Owings Merrill’s “Delta Dome,” a 40,000-seat stadium in Delta Park, to GGN’s radical re-envisioning of Mt Tabor Park. It's a survey of Portland's past ambitions and its current array of design talent!
events.title: Unseen Portland Architecture: the best of Portland design. Never built

events.summary: Stringing Beads / Ensartar Cuentas brings together the work of Orquidia Violeta, Mariela Finvarb, Beatriz Bellorín, and Marisol Valencia in an exhibition that grew from the relationships formed during and after the 2024 Stelo Summer Invitational Residency. Expanded through a year of virtual gatherings, the exhibition reflects on how artistic dialogue continues to shape creative practice beyond the residency itself. Through photography, video, textiles, ceramics, painting, and installation, the artists explore migration, identity, memory, grief, ecology, ancestral knowledge, and care. Like beads threaded together, each work retains its individuality while contributing to a larger conversation about belonging, transformation, and the enduring connections forged through shared experience. events.summary: Chefas Projects is pleased to present Galvanized, the first solo exhibition at the gallery by Portland artist Bobby Adams. On view September 18 through October 17, the exhibition brings together seven new gradient paintings that extend Adams’s ongoing investigation into color, movement, precision, and reduction. Working with hard edges and meticulously calibrated color transitions, Adams constructs paintings that appear at once exacting and elusive. Color becomes both subject and structure: gradients shift across the surface with a measured sense of movement, while simplified compositions heighten the perceptual effects of scale, saturation, and transition. The paintings inhabit a productive space between the mechanical and the handmade, where precision does not eliminate the presence of the artist but makes it more apparent. Adams’s approach is informed by a background outside of traditional art-making. Before turning to painting in 2017, he worked in product development and ran a clothing line for eight years. That experience with materials, systems, color, and visual identity remains embedded in his practice. His paintings share an affinity with the economy and immediacy of graphic design while resisting its fixedness; seemingly simple arrangements become dynamic through subtle shifts in color and proportion. The title Galvanized gestures toward a central tension within the work: the desire to achieve a polished, controlled image alongside the inevitable irregularities of its making. Adams’s paintings are rigorously constructed, but they are not anonymous. Their surfaces hold the evidence of decisions, adjustments, and the physical act of painting. Running through the exhibition is Adams’s longstanding relationship to NASCAR, a significant influence on his upbringing and visual sensibility. The sport’s saturated palettes, speed, spectacle, and graphic intensity provide an unexpected point of departure for paintings that are otherwise characterized by restraint. In California Poppy, this connection is particularly pronounced. Its color relationships carry the visual charge of racing culture while being distilled through Adams’s pared-down formal language. The result is a body of work in which speed is suggested rather than depicted, and where movement emerges from the most economical means. Adams takes visual cues associated with motion, competition, and spectacle and subjects them to the slower, more deliberate logic of abstraction. Galvanized marks an important step in Adams’s relationship with the gallery, following his inclusion in multiple group exhibitions and establishing a sustained presentation of his practice through a focused body of new work.
events.title: BOBBY ADAMS | GALVANIZED

events.summary: Chefas Projects is pleased to present Mercurial, a new solo exhibition by sculptural artist Dan Lam, on view September 18 through October 17, 2026. Bringing together more than twenty new works, the exhibition introduces a heightened metallic sensibility to Lam’s singular sculptural language, with surfaces that suggest chrome, liquid metal, and something less readily identifiable-objects caught somewhere between matter and mutation. Known for sculptures that occupy an uncanny space between the organic and the artificial, Lam approaches form as something fluid, seductive, and alive. In Mercurial, this sensibility takes on a distinctly reflective character. Metallic hues course across the surfaces of the works, emphasizing their bulbous contours, dripping edges, and seemingly unstable forms. Chrome-like finishes catch and distort their surroundings, allowing the sculptures to shift with changes in light, perspective, and proximity. The works appear to ooze, pool, drip, and swell. Their surfaces suggest viscosity while their forms remain resolutely sculptural, creating an intriguing contradiction between solidity and liquidity. They seem less like objects that have been made than organisms in the midst of becoming - alien, tactile, and strangely familiar. This tension is fundamental to Lam’s practice. Her sculptures consistently operate between opposing states: attraction and repulsion, organic and inanimate, soft and hard, seriousness and play. Rather than resolving these contradictions, Lam uses them as points of departure. The resulting forms possess an uncanny immediacy, inviting viewers to move closer even as their unfamiliarity introduces a note of hesitation. In Mercurial, the reflective surfaces intensify this exchange between object and viewer. The sculptures absorb fragments of their environments and return them altered, making the surrounding space part of the work. What initially reads as an autonomous object becomes something more relational-a form that changes depending on where it is encountered and how it is seen. Despite their otherworldly appearance, Lam’s sculptures remain remarkably approachable. Playfulness is central to their charge. The works resist the distance sometimes associated with contemporary sculpture, instead engaging the viewer through color, surface, scale, and a visceral sense of recognition. They are strange without being alienating; experimental without abandoning the pleasures of looking. The title Mercurial evokes both the mutable nature of the works and their affinity with mercury: a substance defined by its fluidity, reflectivity, and ability to transform its appearance in relation to its surroundings. Here, Lam translates those qualities into sculptural form. Her objects appear perpetually in motion, suspended between states, as though their final form has not yet been decided. Across more than twenty new sculptures, Mercurial expands Lam’s investigation of the space between the familiar and the unknown. The works activate the imagination through an intuitive visual language - one based not on representation but on sensation. Their exaggerated forms, seductive surfaces, and ambiguous materiality encourage viewers to project, imagine, and participate. In Lam’s hands, sculpture becomes less a fixed thing than an encounter: part organism, part object, part fantasy. Mercurial embraces that instability, presenting a body of work that is at once polished and unruly, seductive and strange, playful and profound.
events.title: DAN LAM | MERCURIAL

events.summary: Juggle For the Health of It at the 34th Annual Portland Juggling Festival More than a fun challenge, juggling has been scientifically proven to increase neuroplasticity, reduce stress, and improve posture (if only it also did the dishes). Try this 4,000-year-old sport at Reed College’s Aubrey Watzek Sports Center September 25-27. The playful community of Portland Jugglers invites you to “drop everything and juggle” whether you’re a one ball newbie or a practiced pro. The benefits are mental, physical, and social as festival goers shed their clumsiness in workshops for all levels. Plus there are prop venders, practice spaces, and truly unique games like quarter juggling (last one juggling gets them all). If you want to stretch your mind and muscles beyond playing catch with balls and clubs, the festival encourages you to try poi, yoyo, unicycles, hula-hoops, and other props. “We’re very inclusive of toys and people,” says founding Portland Juggler Rhys Thomas. Saturday night’s family-friendly Juggling & Vaudeville Extravaganza on September 26 showcases jaw-dropping skills—and tons of humor—performed by talented local and internationally touring artists. The doors of Kaul Auditorium open at 6:30, with showtime at 7 p.m. Tickets are available online at portlandjugglers.org, as well as on site. A general festival weekend pass with show ticket is $60. Festival only $35. Tickets for just the Juggling and Vaudeville Extravaganza show are $35 for adults, and $30 for children/students/seniors. Complete festival details, schedule, and a full list of special guests and performers are available at portlandjugglers.org.
events.title: Kept Weird: 34th annual Portland Juggling Festival

events.summary: Experience Chapel Voices, an intimate evening of Baroque vocal music in Trinity's luminous Chapel, featuring sopranos Arwen Myers, Amy Stuart Hunn, and Christine Johnson, and baritone Daniel Pickens-Jones. An exciting addition to Trinity's Music Series, Chapel Voices returns following the success of last year's inaugural concert and fundraiser. Chapel Voices 2026 is inspired by the French genre Airs sérieux et à boire ("Serious and Drinking Songs"), a celebrated collection published over 22 years by Parisian publisher Jean-Baptiste Christophe Ballard. At turns graceful, tender, gripping, tuneful, and bawdy, the program spans the rich musical traditions of France, Germany, Italy, and England, exploring the remarkable variety of Baroque vocal music from the 17th and early 18th centuries. The concert features works by J.S. Bach, John Dowland, Heinrich Schütz, Barbara Strozzi, and François Couperin, and ranges from sacred and devotional pieces, including Purcell's The Blessed Virgin's Expostulation, to secular songs of love, reflection, and conviviality, such as a command performance of Scarlatti's stunning Euridice all'inferno by soprano Arwen Myers. Completing the ensemble are Organ Scholar James Walton on Trinity's Italian harpsichord and Ryan Ponto on viola da gamba. While the Cathedral itself inspires awe through its grandeur, soaring architecture, and sense of history, the Chapel offers a different but equally compelling experience: warm, welcoming, and intimate. Its inviting acoustic evokes the scale and atmosphere in which much of this music was originally heard, allowing audiences to encounter these Baroque treasures at close range. Chapel Voices promises an evening of exceptional vocal artistry, historical discovery, and captivating musical storytelling in one of Trinity's most beautiful and inspiring spaces.
events.title: Chapel Voices

events.summary: Written in 1936, this light-hearted comedy has relevance for today in addressing the main theme of finding one’s own way in today’s complex society, while lightly viewing such topics as distrust of government, domestic terrorism and fear of foreign conflicts. “Grandpa” Vanderhof (Robert Lovitz) once worked in the competitive business world. One day, he realized he was unhappy, so he stopped working. Since then, he spends his days catching and raising snakes, watching graduation ceremonies, visiting old friends, and doing whatever else he wants. His daughter Penny (Marilyn Stacey) writes plays simply because a few years ago a typewriter was delivered to the house by accident. His son-in-law Paul Sycamore (Todd Hermanson) spends hours in the basement making illegal fireworks and playing with erector sets. His granddaughter Essie (Bonnie Auguston) sells candy and has been clumsily attempting ballet for over eight years. His grandson-in-law Ed Carmichael (Aiden Brown) plays the xylophone (or tries to) and accidentally distributes Marxist propaganda. Joining this free-for-all are Rheba (Caren Graham), the household cook; her unemployed boyfriend, Donald (Shaun Hennessy); Essie’s opinionated Russian ballet instructor, Mr. Kolenkhov (Mark Schwahn); Olga (Trisha Todd), a Russian Grand Duchess; Gay Wellington (Adrienne Southard), a heavy-drinking actress; Wilbur C. Henderson (Douglas Hout), a forlorn IRS employee; and Mr. De Pinna (Danny Bruno), a deliveryman who arrived 8 years ago and decided to stay. He now helps with the fireworks and dresses in Roman togas to pose for Penny’s portraits. All is somewhat calm until three men from the government (Christopher Sparks, Dan Weiss, and Erik James) visit to investigate Ed’s flyers. In this crazy mix of characters, there is also Alice (Taylor Jean Grady), Penny and Paul’s other daughter and, apparently, the only “normal” family member. She met Tony Kirby (Noah Matthew Rich) at his dad’s Wall Street investment firm, and they’ve fallen in love. Culture shock and fireworks fly when Mr. Kirby (Jeremy Southard) and Mrs. Kirby (Wendy Martel) come to visit. But the message is clear: “Life’s pretty simple if you just relax,” as Grandpa puts it. You Can’t Take It With You is directed by Don Alder. Set design is by Chris Whitten, lighting design is by Demetri Pavlatos, costume design is by Janelle Sutton, prop design is by Allen R. Phillips, the stage manager is Alex Salem, the assistant stage manager is Nat Weinham, and the producer is Steve Knox.
events.title: You Can't Take It With You

events.summary: SEPTEMBER FLIGHT FEATURING 2 SOLOS BY Don Nigro September 11–27 Fri/Sat 7:30, Sun 2 $38 per person Imago Theatre, 17 SE 8th Avenue imagotheatre.com TICKETS https://onthestage.tickets/show/imago-theatre/6a56bc1797fd36b14c05ee83 Tickets also available at the door. Theatre opens one hour before showtime. All seats $38. The show is for mature audiences. The Dark, performed by Joe Cullen (Salomé, Design for Living) and Cincinnati, performed by Diane Slamp (Geography of a Horse Dreamer, Design for Living). Direction by Jerry Mouawad. THE DARK A man in his thirties grapples with a fundamental question: does he truly exist? This dilemma, first encountered at age four, drives the narrative of this ten-page script. Director Jerry Mouawad calls it "the perfect warm-up for Nigro’s work and his intriguing solos, many of which take place in a theatre." CINCINNATI "It’s hard not to feel that this piece was written specifically for Imago," says Slamp, who portrays a lost professor navigating a world of tragedy, sex, and philosophical diatribes. Her diversions reveal a desperate search for redemption amidst personal disaster. "Cincinnati is multi-layered, blending mythology and realism with an ontological examination of life and being," explains Mouawad. "It’s a gem for an audience seeking a new kind of theatre. Don’t let the heavy themes mislead you; this is a small spectacle with humor and high style. I see it as a consciousness tangling with forces of nature, an uncertain reality, and a triad of personas—real or unreal—in a lecture that pushes the boundaries of endurance.” Production Credits: *Light Design:* Ronnie Rantis Costume Design: Laura Helgeson Sound Design: Myrrh Larsen Note: For Mature Audiences In October, Imago returns with October Flight, featuring more solos by Don Nigro.

events.summary: Adapted from Agatha Christie’s classic mystery, this immersive production brings the psychological tension of the classic tale into immediate, breath-held proximity. Our story takes place inside a remote seaside mansion after a violent storm strands ten guests and their hosts. When an eerie accusation recorded on a gramophone accuses each of them of wrongdoing, the guests confront secrets, guilt, and suspicion. Trapped by weather and circumstance, alliances form and fracture… old grievances surface, and rationality gives way to intense fear as each new death raises the stakes. At ETP’s production, you’ll find yourself sitting with the characters within the house itself, among the bedrooms, the dining room, and narrow passages. Experience the shifting power dynamics and mounting claustrophobia as if you were part of the action. Hear whispered confrontations up close, overhear private confessions, and feel the silence before the next crisis. Though the environment surrounds you, the audience is strictly non-participatory — as a silent witness, a “fly on the wall,” you will never be directly addressed by the characters, nor asked to participate. What to expect in performance: \- Tension-driven mystery with tightly controlled pacing and sudden shocks. \- Strong emphasis on atmosphere: storm sound design, flickering lantern and candlelight, thunder, and selective blackout moments. \- Intense emotional scenes: accusations, breakdowns, moral reckonings, and desperate attempts to find the culprit. \- Minimalist, realistic set dressing that transforms the performance space into a lived-in island mansion, with audience seating integrated into set locations (chairs, benches, window alcoves). \- No audience interaction; observers remain silent and stationary throughout each performance. Content warnings: Multiple onstage deaths and depictions of violence (staged, non-graphic). Mature themes and dialogue — recommended for ages 13+ About Experience Theatre Project: Experience Theatre Project is an innovative, immersive theater company based in Aloha, Oregon. Unlike traditional theaters with rows of seats and a proscenium stage, ETP crafts imaginative and fully surrounding narratives, drawing inspiration from both original and classic stories. Our specialty lies in presenting these tales in an unconventional, unexpected fashion, surrounding audiences in the world of the play, similar to a haunted house or a Disney experience. Limiting audiences to sixty or fewer ensures an intimate and memorable experience. Ticket link: www.experiencetheatreproject.org
events.title: ETP Presents Agatha Christie's And Then There Were None

Their sound moves confidently between groove-driven rhythms, layered textures, and sharp, memorable hooks-built to land just as well on a packed dance floor as it does in a focused listening room. With a reputation for engaging performances and a dynamic stage presence, this is a show that rewards both casual listeners and dedicated music fans alike. Inspiration and influence can be seen from the likes of Jimmy Smith, Rahsaan Roland Kirk, The Crusaders, Roy Ayers, The Meters, Hot Tuna, Al Green, George Benson, Funkadelic, Stevie Wonder, The Brothers Johnson, Freddie Hubbard, Frank Zappa, and so many more!! Comprised of lifelong multi-instrumentalists, its members have deep passion for music, as well as deep roots in Portland's music legacy from the historic Day Music Company to the transformative Peak Experience Productions. Expect screaming jams and grooving beats to truly get your mojo buzzing. Specifically designed to enhance your journey, The Light Fantastic will take you higher and higher! Come, Let's Trip The Light Fantastic Together!! www.lightfantasticmusic.com
events.title: The Light Fantastic

events.summary: 7pm doors, 8pm show All ages welcome Jakki and the Pink Smudge Jakki and the Pink Smudge, colloquially known as Smudge, is an indie rock outfit from Portland, Oregon. Our sound has been described as indie-punk-funk, dreamy fuzz rock, and peachy pop rock, but ultimately, we are informed by the intent of just making good music and surrounding ourselves with good people who like it too. For those who have yet to be smudged, you can hear flashes of our inspirations from the gritty twang of Wednesday, lyrical prowess of This is Lorelei, and the suppleness of Slow Pulp, filtered through a voice, style, and stickiness that is entirely our own. Smudge performances were built on a nomadic DIY landscape. The band started as a project by Jakki Wise, taken all over the country by bands and musicians who wanted to play the music together live, known as smudging. Each show took on a new chemistry, allowing the songs to grow, bend, and surprise in real time. This rotating cast became a hallmark of the project and helped fuel its sense of experimentation and play. In 2023, Smudge entered a new chapter with a permanent rhythm section featuring Oliver Lester on bass, Jasper Gill on drums, and Jude Abare on synth. With their debut album released in May 2025 and a solidified live band, Smudge has stepped into this next season with renewed focus, sharper energy, and a sound that continues to build upon itself. Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/jakkiandthepinksmudge/ Spotify: https://open.spotify.com/artist/2PE0MKxlv96ldrmc9Ha3C6 Website: https://jakkiwise.com

events.summary: Celtic Light Orchestra From The Shire September 25, 26, & 27, 2026 Echo Theater 1515 SE 37th Ave, Portland, OR ALL AGES Inviting all Hobbits, Elves, Dwarves, and Wizards to Katie Jane’s Celtic Light Orchestra From The Shire! BACK BY POPULAR DEMAND! This multi-media production promises to be an unforgettable experience for the whole family with beloved melodies from the original Hobbit cartoon, fan favorites from the Lord of the Rings trilogy, iconic Tolkien quotes, rousing Celtic fiddle music, rocking Led Zeppelin arranged for string orchestra, stunning aerial dance, LED lights, dazzling costumes, and more! Featuring Portland’s renowned Celtic fiddle virtuoso, Katie Jane Lubiens! Don’t miss this one-of-a-kind Celtic concert experience, you tricksy hobbitses! About the Celtic Light Orchestra: The Celtic Light Orchestra is the world’s only light up orchestra! Each one-of-a-kind production features rousing Celtic fiddle music played on the group’s revolutionary patented Glow Bowz invention- LED light up violin bows that react to players’ movements and dance with the music. Combined with traditional Celtic instrumentation, Irish step dancing, Celtic folklore, dazzling lights, and theatrical storytelling, each Celtic Light Orchestra production is a can’t miss event for the whole family! The Celtic Light Orchestra is an all-ages, all-inclusive community orchestra founded by Portland-based music teacher and Celtic fiddle virtuoso, Katie Jane Lubiens. The spirited fiddler started the CLO to share her love of Celtic music and culture with audiences of all ages. Many of the Celtic Light Orchestra members are students of Katie Jane, and many are local school music teachers with a shared passion for making Celtic music and traditions accessible to everyone. Learn more about Katie Jane and the Celtic Light Orchestra at www.celticlightorchestra.com

events.summary: The Multnomah Arts Center (MAC) presents A Good Universe Next Door – A redacted past, a precarious present, and an uncertain future, a group exhibition curated by Celeste Noche and Melanie Stevens. On view in the Front & Center Galleries from September 18 through October 17, 2026, the exhibition features new work by four regional artists: Amber Capwell, Ebony Frison, Maryanna Hollomon, and Orlando Almanza. An opening reception will be held Saturday, September 19, from 1–3 p.m., and an artist talk will take place Saturday, October 10 at 2 p.m. Stevens and Noche invited the artists to consider how utopia and dystopia manifest in their lives, and how they interpret these experiences. Through sculpture, photography, printmaking, and painting, the artists offer visions of futures shaped by remembrance, resistance, solidarity, creativity, and care. Ebony Frison approaches utopia and dystopia as “conditions that coexist within the same historical moment.” Working with archival research, printmaking, photography, and artist books, Frison examines how Black histories persist despite erasure, describing utopia as “a practice of rememory—an active engagement with ancestral knowledge, community care, and historical reclamation.” Maryanna Hollomon highlights the aftermath of war for children and the global systems that produce displacement. “A utopia cannot be achieved without working in solidarity with those most oppressed,” she writes. Her work asks viewers to consider militarism’s impact and to imagine new forms of resistance and collective care. Amber Capwell creates sculptural works that envision utopian possibilities through Tarot readings for endangered Pacific Northwest flora and fauna. “These sculptures exist as a reminder to care,” they write. Their work incorporates queer and trans identities as part of an ecological futurism that demands “a utopia existing where we are allowed to live and thrive.” Orlando Almanza imagines futures built on safety, connection, and community. “I dream of a place where my people can have picnics next to the river, to rest, to laugh… and the grandmothers can enjoy their old age, sitting in their rocking chairs on their front porch,” he writes. “Sueño con el día que pueda ver a mi familia reunida, en la tierra que nos vio nacer” (I dream that one day my family can be reunited, in the land that birthed us). The Multnomah Arts Center is located at 7688 SW Capitol Hwy, Portland, OR, 97219. It is open Monday – Thursday 9 a.m. to 9:30 p.m., and Friday – Saturday 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Additional Information: The Multnomah Arts Center is a part of Portland Parks & Recreation. MAC offers programs in a wide range of visual, music, movement, theater, and literary arts at an affordable cost to people of all ages. In addition to this vibrant arts education program, MAC runs a community-based visual arts exhibition program, which includes the MAC Front & Center Galleries. MAC also hosts theatre, music and dance performances, and other special events. The Multnomah Arts Center Association (MACA) is an all-volunteer, 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization that exists to support equity and access to arts education at MAC. MACA provides scholarships, supports community engagements efforts, and provides specialized arts equipment and facility improvements. Their efforts expand opportunities and enhance the experience of students, instructors, and the community at-large. For more information about MAC or MACA, please call 503.823.2787 or visit www.multnomahartscenter.org.

events.summary: PDX CONTEMPORARY ART is pleased to present THE HEROINES, a new exhibition by Seattle-based artist Victoria Haven. For this body of work, Victoria Haven referenced The Heroides, a collection of poems by Ovid written from the perspective of fifteen heroines of Greek and Roman mythology. Using the poems as source material and framework, the works in the exhibition dissect and reassemble mythological narratives into an invented language. The Heroines Alphabet, a series of graphite drawings, uses the title of the show as a system for revealing hidden words. Placed in a grid, Haven connects adjacent letters in ‘The Heroines’ to form new words, some with multiple readings or meanings. The Linguistic Architecture drawings abstract the alphabet further, transforming each letter of the title phrase into dark, inky rectangles with bright scarlet notations. Stripped of the actual letters, the words remain as only an echo of the informing system. The fifteen heroines are further revealed in a large-scale wall drawing with accompanying sound installation which layers incantatory murmurings taken from classical translations and a contemporary adaptation of Ovid’s epistolary poems. Ideas of language, voice, and story continue to unfold throughout the gallery in various forms, including silkscreen prints, mirrored objects, paintings, and a levitating, triangular bronze Penelope sculpture. Join us at the gallery Saturday, September 12th, at 2:30 pm for an artist talk with Victoria Haven and author Claire Dederer discussing the process surrounding this body of work and how it connects to ideas of perception, voice and language in her artist practice.
events.title: THE HEROINES · Victoria Haven

events.summary: Juggle For the Health of It at the 34th Annual Portland Juggling Festival More than a fun challenge, juggling has been scientifically proven to increase neuroplasticity, reduce stress, and improve posture (if only it also did the dishes). Try this 4,000-year-old sport at Reed College’s Aubrey Watzek Sports Center September 25-27. The playful community of Portland Jugglers invites you to “drop everything and juggle” whether you’re a one ball newbie or a practiced pro. The benefits are mental, physical, and social as festival goers shed their clumsiness in workshops for all levels. Plus there are prop venders, practice spaces, and truly unique games like quarter juggling (last one juggling gets them all). If you want to stretch your mind and muscles beyond playing catch with balls and clubs, the festival encourages you to try poi, yoyo, unicycles, hula-hoops, and other props. “We’re very inclusive of toys and people,” says founding Portland Juggler Rhys Thomas. Saturday night’s family-friendly Juggling & Vaudeville Extravaganza on September 26 showcases jaw-dropping skills—and tons of humor—performed by talented local and internationally touring artists. The doors of Kaul Auditorium open at 6:30, with showtime at 7 p.m. Tickets are available online at portlandjugglers.org, as well as on site. A general festival weekend pass with show ticket is $60. Festival only $35. Tickets for just the Juggling and Vaudeville Extravaganza show are $35 for adults, and $30 for children/students/seniors. Complete festival details, schedule, and a full list of special guests and performers are available at portlandjugglers.org.

events.summary: Curated by Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK School and Lisa Jarrett Drawing from the Museum’s collection, this exhibition is co-curated by Lisa Jarrett, an artist, educator, and curator, and the Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK Elementary— a group of 4th and 5th grade curators from KSMoCA. Working from a conversation with notable curators Dr. Lowery Stokes Sims and Dr. Leslie King Hammond, the exhibition engages PAM’s collection in new dialogues shaped by emerging curatorial voices and multigenerational knowledge. From theme and concept development, through work selection, and installation, this community curators project highlights the collaborative nature of curatorial practice and museum work. Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK School \(HTC\) is a KSMoCA project. Students participate directly in shaping exhibitions, positioning them as contributors to the museum, and engaging them as researchers, writers, planners, and curators. Through workshops and field trips, students collaborate with artists, visiting curators, and mentors from Portland State University’s College of the Arts. They research how exhibitions are developed, how artworks are interpreted, and how institutional decisions shape public understanding. Expanded curatorial practice includes visual art, writing, performance, research, publishing, and social practice. Co-founded by Lisa Jarrett and Harrell Fletcher, the project began in 2018 at Harriet Tubman Middle School and continues in its current iteration at Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Elementary School.
events.title: Harriet Tubman Center Museum

events.summary: Inspired by Katherine Ace’s 9 Portraits as the foundational starting point for the exhibition, Nine Women Artists will feature the work of the artists shown in Ace’s portrait painting. All mature artists in their careers and with a significant presence in the Northwest, their work reveals a diverse expression of artistic styles from representation to abstraction. There are rich details in the painting. Most notably on the left hangs Henri Fantin-Latour’s A Studio at Les Batignolles, 1870 \(Musée d’Orsay\). In this painting is a formal gathering of male artists. In response to this painting, Katherine asked her subjects to dress in their studio/work clothes as counterpoint, all marked in their characteristic poses. Other Portland women artists are recognized here through their paintings—a small Sally Haley still life hangs in the background, as well as an Amanda Snyder painting behind Phyllis Yes. And to the far right, we have a glimpse of Lucinda Parker’s very large work. Postcards and newspapers scattered on the floor are the exhibition announcements and reviews highlighting the artists’ works. An epic portrait featuring nine women artists of the Northwest, Ace responded to the lack of self-portraits by women artists in history. From left, the artists are: Laura Ross-Paul, Katherine’s self-portrait seated with phone, Mary Josephson, Judy Cooke, Phyllis Yes, Sharon Bronzan, Shu-Ju Wang, Lucinda Parker, and Sherrie Wolf. All are women artists who have made long careers in Portland. As Ace notes about these women, “They have tenacity, have lived through sexist decades, told they couldn’t really be artists—only fit for sleeping with the professor, expected to subvert themselves to male artist machismo.”
events.title: Nine Women Artists

events.summary: Dashing dachshunds, endless sausages, polka, pilsner, pretzels and more will take over Oaks Park Sept. 25-27 during the park’s ever-popular Oktoberfest. The three-day, family-friendly celebration of autumn will be packed with traditional food and beverages, authentic music and dancing and an array of Oktoberfest activities for revelers of all ages. “Over the years, Oaks Park’s Oktoberfest has grown into one of our most popular celebrations of the year,” said Emily MacKay, Oaks Park’s Marketing and Events Director. “From great food and drinks to live music, Bavarian cooking shows, wiener dog races and even a pretzel toss contest, we have something for everyone.” Oaks Park has been hosting its Oktoberfest since the early 1990s. This year’s festival will feature all the favorites that have made the festival at Oaks Park so popular, including: Food and drink: A range of imported Paulaner beers will be available along with craft ciders and wines. Food vendors include Schnitzel Haus, Brat Barn, Wienerwurst, Eis Hutte, the Buffalo Gap and others. Activities: The three-day fest will feature an all-ages dance floor, Bavarian cooking shows, wiener dog races, a pretzel toss, a condiment art contest, a vendor village, a Chicken Dance contest and more. There will also be the kid-friendly Kinderplatz on Saturday and Sunday, where kids can find fun arts, crafts and music. Music: It’s not Oktoberfest without great polka, and Oaks Park has a full lineup, from The Polkatones and The Tirolean Dancers to The Alpine Echoes and accordionist Elizabeth Wisler. In addition to all the Oktoberfest fun, Oaks Park will have its rides, games and other attractions running at full speed. Gate-only admission for Oktoberfest is $7.50 for those 48” and taller and $4.50 for those under 48”. Gate admission with a Ride Bracelet is $44.45 for guests 48” and taller and $23.45 for anyone under 48”. Infants 2 and under are free. Oaks Park’s classic roller-skating rink and mini golf course will also be available for guests for an additional price. Hours for Oktoberfest at Oaks Park are: 4 p.m. to 10 p.m. Friday, Sept. 25; 11 a.m. to 10 p.m. Saturday, Sept. 26; and 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. Sunday, Sept. 27. Video highlights of last year’s Oktoberfest can be seen here. For more information about this year’s Oktoberfest at Oaks Park, including schedules, activity details and more, visit Oakspark.com.
events.title: Portland's favorite Oktoberfest returns to Oaks Park Sept. 25-27

events.summary: The Northwest’s Original Grapestomping is Coming up! Announcing the 44th Annual St JOSEF’S Grapestomping Festival Sept 26th & 27th, 2026 @ St Josef’s Winery- Canby, (Willamette Valley) Oregon German Style Wines, German Music, German Food & even German Beer.... And lots of Grapestomping! Saturday, Sept 26th and Sunday, September 27th. Open Noon – 5pm. Rain or Shine Featuring - The Gordonaires from Canada- a fun band playing German music and more The festival started in 1983 when there were less than 30 wineries in Oregon. Founders, Josef & Lilli who emigrated from Germany, wanted to pass on a little bit of the harvest spirit to the burgeoning Oregon wine industry. Since running a vineyard and winery is a lot of hard work, they believed it was important to start the busy crush season off with a lighthearted approach. A fun harvest festival with lively music, local foods and of course, stomping grapes in a casual European atmosphere! In addition to Grapestomping contests held throughout the day, the ‘Gordonaires’ a great six-piece German Band will be performing from 1pm to 4:30 pm on Saturday and Sunday. Food includes special house recipe German sausages & homemade sauerkraut, along with other locally made foods. New vintages and special reserve wines will be available by the glass, plus tours with the winemaker and tastings will occur throughout the day. Can we stomp the grapes? Yes! We’re always looking for volunteers to help us stomp! This year you can even reserve a spot to with our VIP Grapestomping Packages. Which includes admission for Two, 2 souvenir glasses, wine tasting or a glass of wine or beer for each. Plus a reserved Grapestomping time for two along with tour with the winemaker and three bottles of wine to take home to enjoy (one red, one white, one sparkling from our current releases). We will also be looking for more Grapestomping volunteers throughout the day. (stompers need to be 21+) And everyone will be able to get a picture of their feet in the grapes. Do we need to make a reservation to attend the event? No- but advance tickets will save you 20%. Advance tickets include a souvenir glass and wine tasting (or glass of wine or beer). Tickets at the door will be $15 and include a souvenir glass. Tickets and VIP packages available @ stjosefswinery.com St Josef’s is one of Oregon’s Wine Pioneers with vineyards planted in 1978 and first legal vintage in 1983. 99 % of production is from the property and the 40 acres of estate vineyards have been awarded ‘Salmon Safe’ designation and are tended without the use of irrigation, harsh chemicals or pesticide with goats & llamas helping with the landscaping. The event will feature all of the current releases; selections of reserve wines and sparkling wines – including the latest releases of award winning Lilli Sparkling wines, St Josef’s Chardonnay & Kitara Reserve Syrah. The 44th Annual St Josef’s Grapestomping Festival Hours are noon-5pm both days- Saturday Sept 26th and Sunday 27th 2026. St Josef’s is located at 28836 S Barlow Road, Canby, Oregon. (503) 651-3190 stjosefswinery.com Admission is $15 for those over 21, and includes souvenir wine glass. (Children under 18 are free if supervised, $500 otherwise). Advance admission tickets and VIP stomp packages are available. And bottle discounts for new releases and library reserve wines For more information contact - info@stjosefswinery.com
events.title: St Josef’s Grapestomping Festival 2026

events.summary: Chefas Projects is pleased to present Galvanized, the first solo exhibition at the gallery by Portland artist Bobby Adams. On view September 18 through October 17, the exhibition brings together seven new gradient paintings that extend Adams’s ongoing investigation into color, movement, precision, and reduction. Working with hard edges and meticulously calibrated color transitions, Adams constructs paintings that appear at once exacting and elusive. Color becomes both subject and structure: gradients shift across the surface with a measured sense of movement, while simplified compositions heighten the perceptual effects of scale, saturation, and transition. The paintings inhabit a productive space between the mechanical and the handmade, where precision does not eliminate the presence of the artist but makes it more apparent. Adams’s approach is informed by a background outside of traditional art-making. Before turning to painting in 2017, he worked in product development and ran a clothing line for eight years. That experience with materials, systems, color, and visual identity remains embedded in his practice. His paintings share an affinity with the economy and immediacy of graphic design while resisting its fixedness; seemingly simple arrangements become dynamic through subtle shifts in color and proportion. The title Galvanized gestures toward a central tension within the work: the desire to achieve a polished, controlled image alongside the inevitable irregularities of its making. Adams’s paintings are rigorously constructed, but they are not anonymous. Their surfaces hold the evidence of decisions, adjustments, and the physical act of painting. Running through the exhibition is Adams’s longstanding relationship to NASCAR, a significant influence on his upbringing and visual sensibility. The sport’s saturated palettes, speed, spectacle, and graphic intensity provide an unexpected point of departure for paintings that are otherwise characterized by restraint. In California Poppy, this connection is particularly pronounced. Its color relationships carry the visual charge of racing culture while being distilled through Adams’s pared-down formal language. The result is a body of work in which speed is suggested rather than depicted, and where movement emerges from the most economical means. Adams takes visual cues associated with motion, competition, and spectacle and subjects them to the slower, more deliberate logic of abstraction. Galvanized marks an important step in Adams’s relationship with the gallery, following his inclusion in multiple group exhibitions and establishing a sustained presentation of his practice through a focused body of new work.
events.title: BOBBY ADAMS | GALVANIZED

events.summary: Chefas Projects is pleased to present Mercurial, a new solo exhibition by sculptural artist Dan Lam, on view September 18 through October 17, 2026. Bringing together more than twenty new works, the exhibition introduces a heightened metallic sensibility to Lam’s singular sculptural language, with surfaces that suggest chrome, liquid metal, and something less readily identifiable-objects caught somewhere between matter and mutation. Known for sculptures that occupy an uncanny space between the organic and the artificial, Lam approaches form as something fluid, seductive, and alive. In Mercurial, this sensibility takes on a distinctly reflective character. Metallic hues course across the surfaces of the works, emphasizing their bulbous contours, dripping edges, and seemingly unstable forms. Chrome-like finishes catch and distort their surroundings, allowing the sculptures to shift with changes in light, perspective, and proximity. The works appear to ooze, pool, drip, and swell. Their surfaces suggest viscosity while their forms remain resolutely sculptural, creating an intriguing contradiction between solidity and liquidity. They seem less like objects that have been made than organisms in the midst of becoming - alien, tactile, and strangely familiar. This tension is fundamental to Lam’s practice. Her sculptures consistently operate between opposing states: attraction and repulsion, organic and inanimate, soft and hard, seriousness and play. Rather than resolving these contradictions, Lam uses them as points of departure. The resulting forms possess an uncanny immediacy, inviting viewers to move closer even as their unfamiliarity introduces a note of hesitation. In Mercurial, the reflective surfaces intensify this exchange between object and viewer. The sculptures absorb fragments of their environments and return them altered, making the surrounding space part of the work. What initially reads as an autonomous object becomes something more relational-a form that changes depending on where it is encountered and how it is seen. Despite their otherworldly appearance, Lam’s sculptures remain remarkably approachable. Playfulness is central to their charge. The works resist the distance sometimes associated with contemporary sculpture, instead engaging the viewer through color, surface, scale, and a visceral sense of recognition. They are strange without being alienating; experimental without abandoning the pleasures of looking. The title Mercurial evokes both the mutable nature of the works and their affinity with mercury: a substance defined by its fluidity, reflectivity, and ability to transform its appearance in relation to its surroundings. Here, Lam translates those qualities into sculptural form. Her objects appear perpetually in motion, suspended between states, as though their final form has not yet been decided. Across more than twenty new sculptures, Mercurial expands Lam’s investigation of the space between the familiar and the unknown. The works activate the imagination through an intuitive visual language - one based not on representation but on sensation. Their exaggerated forms, seductive surfaces, and ambiguous materiality encourage viewers to project, imagine, and participate. In Lam’s hands, sculpture becomes less a fixed thing than an encounter: part organism, part object, part fantasy. Mercurial embraces that instability, presenting a body of work that is at once polished and unruly, seductive and strange, playful and profound.
events.title: DAN LAM | MERCURIAL

There will be Pee-wee Universe costume contests, Pee-wee look-alike (“I know you are, but what am I?”) and laugh-alike contests, a Pee-wee’s Playhouse trivia competition, a ‘Tequila’ dance-off, and a cat scavenger hunt! Cat scavenger hunt?! The Pee-wee Pub Crawl is a benefit for PDX Cat Trapper. PDX Cat Trapper is a grassroots, 100% volunteer-driven feral cat rescue group. Not so fun fact: A single unaltered cat and all her offspring having a litter of 4 each over a 10-year period, results in a startling 1,398,101 cats. PDX Cat Trapper is interrupting the alarming feral cat reproductive cycle and humanely supports our area’s community cats. PDX Cat Trapper practices ‘trap-neuter-return,’ and are responsible for hundreds, if not thousands, of community cats getting fixed every year. They also organize cat colony medical care and feeding services though their all-volunteer grassroots outreach program. PDX Cat Trapper is a registered 501(c)(3) charity, and will receive 75% of the proceeds from ticket sales to the PHPC, as well as cash donations collected from the public via donation jars at the participating bars. . PDX Cat Trapper was chosen not only because the organizers of the Pee-wee Pub Crawl are all great cat lovers, but so was Pee-wee Herman! Paul Reubens was a lifelong animal lover, most especially, of cats. When he passed away, he was the loving cat dad of an untouchable feral, Samantha Reuben-Tenderheart, whom he rescued and for whom he built a large catio, when she made it clear she was not to be an indoor cat. Samantha now lives with one of his best friends, who just happens to be the internet’s famous The Kitten Lady! There will be PDX Cat Trapper cash donation jars stationed at each of our bar stops and the public at large will be encouraged to donate to this very worthy cause. The Pee-wee Pub Crawl will be a fun way to spend a Saturday afternoon reconnecting with one of your old Saturday morning favorites, while connecting with other local Pee-wee Herman fans and cat lovers, alike! Pee-wee Pub Crawl participating bars will create their own Pee-wee Herman inspired drink and food specials. Large Marge-aritas and Ice Cream Soup, anyone? The Pee-wee Pub Crawl is the brainchild of the Paul Reubens Pacific Northwest fan club founder, Meredith Walter, and is being organized and led by Jen Lane, of Portland’s beloved BarFly Magazine and BarFly Bar Tours. BarFly conducted dozens of pub crawls for hundreds of guests, every year during its 20 years in the Portland scene (BarFly quickly succumbed to COVID, and ceased operations in 2020). The Pee-wee Pub Crawl will be a chance to recreate, and perhaps even remember, the BarFly Tour experience The Pee-wee Pub Crawl will be held on Saturday, September 26th, 2026, from 3-9pm. All of the bars will be in the Division/Clinton neighborhood. Participants will be traveling between stops on foot or non-motorized wheels (no driving, please!). This will be a 21 and up, only, event. Advance tickets are required, and are available for purchase at https://peeweepubcrawl.com/. 75% of proceeds from ticket sales will be donated to PDX Cat Trapper.
events.title: Pee-wee Pub Crawl - a fundraiser for PDX Cat Trapper

events.summary: Founded in 2025 by award-winning classical guitar virtuoso and Artistic Director, Tye Austin, M.M., Wilder Frets: Classical Guitar in the Wilderness is a fiscally sponsored nonprofit concert series presenting open-air classical guitar concerts staged in the wilderness of the Pacific Northwest. From August 1 through October 1, Oregon native Tye Austin will perform more than 30 intimate outdoor concerts across 15 of Oregon's most breathtaking state parks—from coastal bluffs to old-growth forests, red rock canyons, thundering waterfalls, vineyards, and ranches. Audiences will experience world-class live music performances through our signature Wilder Sound wireless headphone technology, allowing every guest to enjoy crystal-clear audio while remaining immersed in the beauty of the natural world up to a 1/4 mile radius from the stage. Wilder Frets is more than a concert series. It is a community movement dedicated to making exceptional live music concerts and masterclasses accessible to everyone. Every ticket purchased helps support our growing community initiatives, including: Fret Not Tickets Program, providing complimentary concert tickets to individuals and families facing financial barriers. The Free Frets Initiative, donating free classical guitars, free masterclasses, and mentorship to at-risk from rural, tribal, and urban communities throughout Oregon. Our inaugural season has been made possible through the generosity of our season sponsors and community partners such as Heartbeat Silent Disco, Community Beats, Willamette Valley Music Company, the Maslow Project, and Oregon State Parks who believe that arts, education, conservation, and public access belong together. Whether you're an experienced concertgoer, an outdoor adventurer, or simply looking for a meaningful way to spend an evening, Wilder Frets offers an unforgettable experience unlike anything else in the Pacific Northwest. Join us this season and discover why music sounds even more extraordinary in the great outdoors. View complete tour schedule and purchase tickets online only at www.wilderfrets.org/tour
events.title: Wilder Frets: Classical Guitar in the Wilderness - Inaugural Concert Season

THE EXPERIENCE Join Oscar-nominated production designer Karen Murphy in conversation with interior designer Andee Hess for an evening exploring Murphy's journey from architecture to the world of film. Through behind-the-scenes stories and career reflections, Murphy will share how spaces shape storytelling and reveal the creative process behind designing environments that influence character, emotion, and narrative on screen. This conversation will unpack the powerful relationship between architecture, interiors, and cinematic storytelling, offering a rare glimpse into the art of creating unforgettable worlds. Whether you're passionate about film, design, architecture, or the creative process, this conversation promises inspiration from one of the industry's most accomplished production designers. Want to brush up on Karen's work? Catch THE BRIDE! at a 4 p.m. screening in advance of the talk. ON STAGE: Karen Murphy Karen Murphy is an Australian production designer now based in the United States. Originally trained in architecture, she transitioned to film after working on Baz Luhrmann's Moulin Rouge, which cemented her commitment to the industry. She went on to art direct major films such as The Chronicles of Narnia: The Lion, the Witch, and the Wardrobe, Australia, and The Kite Runner, the latter earning her Art Directors Guild nominations. Murphy has collaborated with Luhrmann and Catherine Martin on films including The Great Gatsby and Elvis, earning recognition from BAFTA, the Art Directors Guild, and the Academy. Her production design credits also include A Star Is Born, Queen & Slim, The Light Between Oceans, Chevalier, and The Order. Recently, she designed Maggie Gyllenhaal's The Bride! and A24's Enemies, which is now in post-production. Karen Murphy's expertise extends beyond film into commercials, interior design, and creative direction, showcasing her versatility in visual storytelling. ON STAGE: Andee Hess Andee Hess is a renowned interior designer known for concept-driven work shaped by a rigorous understanding of material, form, and spatial experience. With a background in welding and a BS in Interior Design, she founded her studio Osmose Design in Portland in 2008. Andee's innovative perspective on spatial design and crafting unique experiences has earned her recognition within the international design community, including features in leading publications. Dubbed "Portland's Secret Design Weapon" by Architectural Digest, Andee's portfolio showcases work for high-profile brands and individuals. Her notable commercial clients include Stumptown, Salt & Straw, and Smith Tea. Andee believes in the transformative power of compelling environments.

events.summary: Glen Hansard, the Irish songwriter, poet, storyteller and bard, was a musician's musician. Most well-known for the Oscar-winning music from the indie film 'Once', including the song Falling Slowly, Glen's imprint on independent folk and rock spread much farther than the night of the Oscars. From street busking, to his Irish rock band The Frames, to his collaboration with Markéta Irglová in the Swell Season, to his solo work that shaped the last two decades of his career, Glen's songwriting had a backbone of honesty that can be hard to find. His dedication to the spirit and mysticism of song inspired thousands of independent artists the world over to find a hopeful, more vulnerable side, and express themselves through whatever artistic means they have. In the wake of his untimely passing on July 29th, 2026 from a motorcycle accident, Glen's positive impact was seen in the outpouring of grief across the world. Portland friends and fans are gathering for a celebration of life and songs for Glen Hansard with a night of song and poetry from some of Portland's favorite local songwriters at the Alberta Rose Theatre. Featured performers include: The Druthers Olivia Awbrey Dan Klee Idea The Artist Rebecca McDade Margaret Wehr Nathan James Earle Chasing Ebenezer Arran Fagan Jacob Miller and more! Whether you're new to Glen's incredible catalogue, familiar with deep cuts from The Frames, or want to sing Falling Slowly in camaraderie with fellow fans, the evening will pay tribute to the arc of Glen's work from beginning to end. Please join us to celebrate the long-lasting music of one of Ireland's \(and Portland's\) most well-loved musicians. Rest In Peace, Glen. Minors ok when accompanied by a parent or guardian. events.summary: Step inside Botticelli’s *Primavera* for an intimate evening of Renaissance music, myth, and philosophy. Guided by Hermes, this performance moves through the spirit of the painting. Our project began from a question at the heart of the Renaissance: what if music, poetry, myth, and philosophy were not separate, but a practice that renews the soul? Inspired by the world of the Florentine Camerata—the musical Academy whose experiments in ancient drama, song, and expressive speech helped give birth to early opera—and by the Neoplatonic revival of Plato, Ficino, Pico, and the ancient theologians, La Primavera explores music as a spiritual and philosophical exercise. Featuring live music, including works by Monteverdi and his contemporaries, La Primavera combines song, projected image, and short philosophical interludes inspired by Plato, Ficino, Pico, Iamblichus, Diotima, Aphrodite, and Eros. These interludes are not lectures, but listening invitations—brief moments that prepare the audience to hear the music and see the painting differently. La Primavera, Palinode's first public performance in Portland, has been developed through a series of workshops that brought together professional musicians and philosophers, drawing upon a form of vital play where philosophy, music, image, myth and live performance come together as a shared ritual of renewal. Come ready to listen, look, and enter the garden. Program Preview Prelude & Philosophical Introduction: Entering the Garden of Remembrance and Renewal Music: Claudio Monteverdi, L’Orfeo Toccata and ritornelli Philosophy: Hermes, Timaeus, Marsilio Ficino I. Winter’s End, Zephyr’s Return: Cloris’s Initiation into the Mysteries of Love Music: Claudio Monteverdi, "Zefiro torna” from L'Orfeo; “Lamento d’Arianna” from L’Arianna Philosophical Interlude: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola II. The Blossoming Spring: Flora’s Abundance Music:, Luzzasco Luzzaschi, “O primavera”; Giovanni Girolamo Kapsberger, Instrumental "canario" Philosophical Interlude: Iamblichus III. The Heat of Summer: The Graces Inspiring Us to Love Music: Barbara Strozzi, “Le tre Gratie à Venere” Philosophical Interlude: Alcibiades IV. Hermes & Diotima’s Call to the Ascension of More Than Apollo Music: Giovanni Girolamo Kapsberger, Toccata seconda arpeggiata; Claudio Monteverdi, “Parch'a lo sdegno” from L’Orfeo Philosophical Interlude: Diotima of Mantinea V. The Ever Fruitful Present: Aphrodite Moves Eros Music: Claudio Monteverdi, “Scendiam, scendiam” from L’incoronazione di Poppea'; “Pur ti miro” from L’incoronazione di Poppea; L’Orfeo ritornello Philosophical Interlude: Diotima of Matinea
events.title: La Primavera: A Night of Renaissance Music, Myth, and Philosophy

events.summary: Written in 1936, this light-hearted comedy has relevance for today in addressing the main theme of finding one’s own way in today’s complex society, while lightly viewing such topics as distrust of government, domestic terrorism and fear of foreign conflicts. “Grandpa” Vanderhof (Robert Lovitz) once worked in the competitive business world. One day, he realized he was unhappy, so he stopped working. Since then, he spends his days catching and raising snakes, watching graduation ceremonies, visiting old friends, and doing whatever else he wants. His daughter Penny (Marilyn Stacey) writes plays simply because a few years ago a typewriter was delivered to the house by accident. His son-in-law Paul Sycamore (Todd Hermanson) spends hours in the basement making illegal fireworks and playing with erector sets. His granddaughter Essie (Bonnie Auguston) sells candy and has been clumsily attempting ballet for over eight years. His grandson-in-law Ed Carmichael (Aiden Brown) plays the xylophone (or tries to) and accidentally distributes Marxist propaganda. Joining this free-for-all are Rheba (Caren Graham), the household cook; her unemployed boyfriend, Donald (Shaun Hennessy); Essie’s opinionated Russian ballet instructor, Mr. Kolenkhov (Mark Schwahn); Olga (Trisha Todd), a Russian Grand Duchess; Gay Wellington (Adrienne Southard), a heavy-drinking actress; Wilbur C. Henderson (Douglas Hout), a forlorn IRS employee; and Mr. De Pinna (Danny Bruno), a deliveryman who arrived 8 years ago and decided to stay. He now helps with the fireworks and dresses in Roman togas to pose for Penny’s portraits. All is somewhat calm until three men from the government (Christopher Sparks, Dan Weiss, and Erik James) visit to investigate Ed’s flyers. In this crazy mix of characters, there is also Alice (Taylor Jean Grady), Penny and Paul’s other daughter and, apparently, the only “normal” family member. She met Tony Kirby (Noah Matthew Rich) at his dad’s Wall Street investment firm, and they’ve fallen in love. Culture shock and fireworks fly when Mr. Kirby (Jeremy Southard) and Mrs. Kirby (Wendy Martel) come to visit. But the message is clear: “Life’s pretty simple if you just relax,” as Grandpa puts it. You Can’t Take It With You is directed by Don Alder. Set design is by Chris Whitten, lighting design is by Demetri Pavlatos, costume design is by Janelle Sutton, prop design is by Allen R. Phillips, the stage manager is Alex Salem, the assistant stage manager is Nat Weinham, and the producer is Steve Knox.
events.title: You Can't Take It With You

events.summary: SEPTEMBER FLIGHT FEATURING 2 SOLOS BY Don Nigro September 11–27 Fri/Sat 7:30, Sun 2 $38 per person Imago Theatre, 17 SE 8th Avenue imagotheatre.com TICKETS https://onthestage.tickets/show/imago-theatre/6a56bc1797fd36b14c05ee83 Tickets also available at the door. Theatre opens one hour before showtime. All seats $38. The show is for mature audiences. The Dark, performed by Joe Cullen (Salomé, Design for Living) and Cincinnati, performed by Diane Slamp (Geography of a Horse Dreamer, Design for Living). Direction by Jerry Mouawad. THE DARK A man in his thirties grapples with a fundamental question: does he truly exist? This dilemma, first encountered at age four, drives the narrative of this ten-page script. Director Jerry Mouawad calls it "the perfect warm-up for Nigro’s work and his intriguing solos, many of which take place in a theatre." CINCINNATI "It’s hard not to feel that this piece was written specifically for Imago," says Slamp, who portrays a lost professor navigating a world of tragedy, sex, and philosophical diatribes. Her diversions reveal a desperate search for redemption amidst personal disaster. "Cincinnati is multi-layered, blending mythology and realism with an ontological examination of life and being," explains Mouawad. "It’s a gem for an audience seeking a new kind of theatre. Don’t let the heavy themes mislead you; this is a small spectacle with humor and high style. I see it as a consciousness tangling with forces of nature, an uncertain reality, and a triad of personas—real or unreal—in a lecture that pushes the boundaries of endurance.” Production Credits: *Light Design:* Ronnie Rantis Costume Design: Laura Helgeson Sound Design: Myrrh Larsen Note: For Mature Audiences In October, Imago returns with October Flight, featuring more solos by Don Nigro.

events.summary: Adapted from Agatha Christie’s classic mystery, this immersive production brings the psychological tension of the classic tale into immediate, breath-held proximity. Our story takes place inside a remote seaside mansion after a violent storm strands ten guests and their hosts. When an eerie accusation recorded on a gramophone accuses each of them of wrongdoing, the guests confront secrets, guilt, and suspicion. Trapped by weather and circumstance, alliances form and fracture… old grievances surface, and rationality gives way to intense fear as each new death raises the stakes. At ETP’s production, you’ll find yourself sitting with the characters within the house itself, among the bedrooms, the dining room, and narrow passages. Experience the shifting power dynamics and mounting claustrophobia as if you were part of the action. Hear whispered confrontations up close, overhear private confessions, and feel the silence before the next crisis. Though the environment surrounds you, the audience is strictly non-participatory — as a silent witness, a “fly on the wall,” you will never be directly addressed by the characters, nor asked to participate. What to expect in performance: \- Tension-driven mystery with tightly controlled pacing and sudden shocks. \- Strong emphasis on atmosphere: storm sound design, flickering lantern and candlelight, thunder, and selective blackout moments. \- Intense emotional scenes: accusations, breakdowns, moral reckonings, and desperate attempts to find the culprit. \- Minimalist, realistic set dressing that transforms the performance space into a lived-in island mansion, with audience seating integrated into set locations (chairs, benches, window alcoves). \- No audience interaction; observers remain silent and stationary throughout each performance. Content warnings: Multiple onstage deaths and depictions of violence (staged, non-graphic). Mature themes and dialogue — recommended for ages 13+ About Experience Theatre Project: Experience Theatre Project is an innovative, immersive theater company based in Aloha, Oregon. Unlike traditional theaters with rows of seats and a proscenium stage, ETP crafts imaginative and fully surrounding narratives, drawing inspiration from both original and classic stories. Our specialty lies in presenting these tales in an unconventional, unexpected fashion, surrounding audiences in the world of the play, similar to a haunted house or a Disney experience. Limiting audiences to sixty or fewer ensures an intimate and memorable experience. Ticket link: www.experiencetheatreproject.org
events.title: ETP Presents Agatha Christie's And Then There Were None

events.summary: Juggle For the Health of It at the 34th Annual Portland Juggling Festival More than a fun challenge, juggling has been scientifically proven to increase neuroplasticity, reduce stress, and improve posture (if only it also did the dishes). Try this 4,000-year-old sport at Reed College’s Aubrey Watzek Sports Center September 25-27. The playful community of Portland Jugglers invites you to “drop everything and juggle” whether you’re a one ball newbie or a practiced pro. The benefits are mental, physical, and social as festival goers shed their clumsiness in workshops for all levels. Plus there are prop venders, practice spaces, and truly unique games like quarter juggling (last one juggling gets them all). If you want to stretch your mind and muscles beyond playing catch with balls and clubs, the festival encourages you to try poi, yoyo, unicycles, hula-hoops, and other props. “We’re very inclusive of toys and people,” says founding Portland Juggler Rhys Thomas. Saturday night’s family-friendly Juggling & Vaudeville Extravaganza on September 26 showcases jaw-dropping skills—and tons of humor—performed by talented local and internationally touring artists. The doors of Kaul Auditorium open at 6:30, with showtime at 7 p.m. Tickets are available online at portlandjugglers.org, as well as on site. A general festival weekend pass with show ticket is $60. Festival only $35. Tickets for just the Juggling and Vaudeville Extravaganza show are $35 for adults, and $30 for children/students/seniors. Complete festival details, schedule, and a full list of special guests and performers are available at portlandjugglers.org.
events.title: Kept Weird: 34th annual Portland Juggling Festival

events.summary: Every writer has moments that seem larger than themselves: a night sky, a death, a first encounter with art, a dream, a sentence in a book, a city seen from above, a strange conversation, a childhood image that never stopped working. This one-day workshop helps writers return to one such moment and begin shaping it into literary material. We will discuss a few brief examples of writing that moves from concrete scene to large question. Then participants will work through a guided sequence: re-entering the sensory scene, locating the pivot where perception changed, naming the question the scene still asks, and drafting a short speculative passage that moves between lived detail and wider meaning. This is a generative class rather than a critique workshop. Writers will leave with new pages, a set of prompts for continued work, and a clearer sense of how large ideas can arise from concrete experience. The atmosphere will be supportive, exploratory, and craft-centered: serious play for writers who want to risk wonder without losing the page. Class outcomes Identify one fundamental scene or image that can become literary material. Draft a short speculative passage rooted in sensory detail. Practice moving from scene to question without over-explaining. Learn a simple revision method for deepening image, voice, and structure. Leave with prompts for continuing the piece after class. Access Program We want our writing classes and seminars to be accessible to everyone, regardless of income and background. We understand that our tuition structure can present obstacles for some people. Our Access Program offers writing class and seminar tuitions at a reduced rate. Most writing classes have at least one access spot available. Please apply here for access rate tuition. Contact Susan Moore at susan@literary-arts.org if you have questions. Liaison position Every in-person class and seminar at Literary Arts has one liaison position. Liaisons perform specific duties for each class meeting. If you are a liaison for a class or seminar, the full amount of your tuition is covered by Literary Arts. Apply here for the liaison position.
events.title: Fundamental Scenes: A Speculative Writing Workshop

events.summary: Curated by Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK School and Lisa Jarrett Drawing from the Museum’s collection, this exhibition is co-curated by Lisa Jarrett, an artist, educator, and curator, and the Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK Elementary— a group of 4th and 5th grade curators from KSMoCA. Working from a conversation with notable curators Dr. Lowery Stokes Sims and Dr. Leslie King Hammond, the exhibition engages PAM’s collection in new dialogues shaped by emerging curatorial voices and multigenerational knowledge. From theme and concept development, through work selection, and installation, this community curators project highlights the collaborative nature of curatorial practice and museum work. Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK School \(HTC\) is a KSMoCA project. Students participate directly in shaping exhibitions, positioning them as contributors to the museum, and engaging them as researchers, writers, planners, and curators. Through workshops and field trips, students collaborate with artists, visiting curators, and mentors from Portland State University’s College of the Arts. They research how exhibitions are developed, how artworks are interpreted, and how institutional decisions shape public understanding. Expanded curatorial practice includes visual art, writing, performance, research, publishing, and social practice. Co-founded by Lisa Jarrett and Harrell Fletcher, the project began in 2018 at Harriet Tubman Middle School and continues in its current iteration at Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Elementary School.
events.title: Harriet Tubman Center Museum

events.summary: Inspired by Katherine Ace’s 9 Portraits as the foundational starting point for the exhibition, Nine Women Artists will feature the work of the artists shown in Ace’s portrait painting. All mature artists in their careers and with a significant presence in the Northwest, their work reveals a diverse expression of artistic styles from representation to abstraction. There are rich details in the painting. Most notably on the left hangs Henri Fantin-Latour’s A Studio at Les Batignolles, 1870 \(Musée d’Orsay\). In this painting is a formal gathering of male artists. In response to this painting, Katherine asked her subjects to dress in their studio/work clothes as counterpoint, all marked in their characteristic poses. Other Portland women artists are recognized here through their paintings—a small Sally Haley still life hangs in the background, as well as an Amanda Snyder painting behind Phyllis Yes. And to the far right, we have a glimpse of Lucinda Parker’s very large work. Postcards and newspapers scattered on the floor are the exhibition announcements and reviews highlighting the artists’ works. An epic portrait featuring nine women artists of the Northwest, Ace responded to the lack of self-portraits by women artists in history. From left, the artists are: Laura Ross-Paul, Katherine’s self-portrait seated with phone, Mary Josephson, Judy Cooke, Phyllis Yes, Sharon Bronzan, Shu-Ju Wang, Lucinda Parker, and Sherrie Wolf. All are women artists who have made long careers in Portland. As Ace notes about these women, “They have tenacity, have lived through sexist decades, told they couldn’t really be artists—only fit for sleeping with the professor, expected to subvert themselves to male artist machismo.”
events.title: Nine Women Artists
