events.summary: Jesse Preis debuts The Raven, a chamber opera composed for three voices and chamber ensemble from Edgar Allan Poe’s poem of the same name, directed by Melory Mirashrafi. In this opera, the narrator (split into two characters to capture the perspective of the Past and the Current at two different stages in life) deals with the loss of a loved one. These complicated, painful, and even terrifying emotions become personified through the character of the Raven. This work is composed with no specific voice types tied to the characters - anyone able to sing the part can and should sing them. This is a groundbreaking composing technique that unties the binds of gendered characters and allows vocalists to portray a character of any gender that is authentic to them and suits their voice. Preis seeks to expand our understanding of vocal writing to go beyond the gendered conventions of soprano, mezzo-soprano, tenor, and bass-baritone, and posits a world where characters are simply written and performed by a wide variety of voices.
events.title: The Raven

events.summary: For 30 years, Willamette Riverkeeper has worked to protect, restore, and connect people to the Willamette River. That work has only been possible because of people like you. ﻿Now it's time to celebrate! Join us aboard the iconic Portland Spirit for a memorable evening cruise as we honor three decades of conservation, community, and impact—and look ahead to the next chapter of caring for our river. Your evening includes:﻿﻿ Scenic cruise on the Willamette River Exclusive access to the Columbia Deck and ship bow Delicious appetizers Live music Stories and reflections from 30 years of impact Silent auction A chance to celebrate with the community that made it all possible Cash bar﻿ This is more than an anniversary. It's a celebration of the river we all love and the people who have helped protect it for future generations. While the evening will honor the leaders, volunteers, partners, and supporters who built this organization, it is equally about building the future of Willamette Riverkeeper. We hope you will join us, not only to celebrate where we have been, but to invest in where we are going. ﻿﻿ All ages welcome! A 30th anniversary is traditionally known as the Pearl Anniversary a celebration of wisdom, resilience, and beauty that grows over time. We view this as a fitting symbol for our celebration, though in our case, another "pearl" comes to mind. Hidden beneath the waters of the Willamette lives the Western Pearlshell Mussel, a species whose presence speaks to water quality and river health. Like these remarkable mussels, our greatest work often happens quietly, beneath the surface. For 30 years, supporters like you have helped build a healthier, more resilient Willamette—one restoration project, one paddle trip, one volunteer event, one protected river mile at a time. Western Pearlshell mussels can live more than 100 years. We aim to follow their example. Together, we are cultivating a legacy of river health and community that will endure for generations.
events.title: Willamette Riverkeeper 30th Anniversary

events.summary: Portland, OR — North 45 Pub is turning 20, and the Northwest Portland neighborhood staple is celebrating by going back to where it all began. On Saturday, October 3 at 7 p.m., North 45 invites longtime regulars, friends, neighbors, and new faces to raise a glass and throw it back to 2006 with an evening of music, food, drinks, and plenty of nostalgia. There is no cover charge. The anniversary celebration will feature a DJ spinning music inspired by 2006, along with a special menu bringing back one of North 45’s longtime favorites: mussels and frites in several of the “greatest hits,” variations. The dish will be paired with a selection of Belgian beers, offering guests a taste of the international influence that has always been part of North 45’s identity. For two decades, North 45 has been a gathering place for Northwest Portland. The space recently got a fresh look, but it remains a neighborhood pub where friends meet for a drink, fans gather for the big game, and countless memories are made. From first dates and first kisses to birthdays, reunions, celebrations, and everyday nights with friends, the pub has been part of the neighborhood fabric since opening its doors in 2006. “We wouldn’t be here for 20 years without the people who have walked through our doors,” said Josh Johnston. “This celebration is about thanking our patrons, friends, neighbors, and employees who have been part of the North 45 story.” Guests are invited to come ready to embrace the era, bring their favorite memories, and celebrate two decades of good food, drinks, music, and company. THE EXPERIENCE Festival Picks brings together eleven films from nine countries that show just how many ways dance can tell a story and where dance film is now. What ties these films together isn't a single style or theme; it's the exploration that movement can express something words can't. Each filmmaker has a different voice, and that's what makes watching them together so rewarding. This year's collection travels from Colombia, Norway, South Korea, France, Canada, Switzerland, Czechia, Argentina, and the USA, inviting us into eleven distinct worlds, all connected through the universal language of dance. Please note there are flashing lights/strobe effects during the film Boys a Bug. ON SCREEN: Festival Picks: 10 Years of PDFF Más Glow | Directed by Laura Steiner & Choreography by Arci, Lucy Cobaleda, Valentina Ávila, and Valentina Hadad | 3:37 | Colombia - Acrylic nails, pink everything, and the faint sound of a bolero. Más Glow speaks to preconceived notions of beauty, the rules imposed on the female body, and the power in taking up space. As gestures unravel inside a nail salon and dance shifts toward monstrous movement, four women break the rules of how they should behave. VEKK | Directed by Thea Bay and Simon M. Valentine & Choreography by Thea Bay | 6:10 | Norway - A dance film about miscommunication and living in different realities. CE QI NOUS LIE | Directed by Damien Bourletsis | 4:55 | France - What if, within the breath of one body, the echo of another was already resonating? In a vital surge where every movement becomes a cry, nine dancers unveil their inner struggle across shifting landscapes: sea, cliff, city, dance studio, ancient theatre. Nine singular territories. Each surrenders to raw improvisation - a moment of questioning rooted in their intimate space - where movement becomes the language of urgency: to be, to resist, to exist. Bodies answer, intertwine, and merge in an organic continuity, weaving bridges between their solitary battles. Living echoes of an invisible geometry, uniting bodies beyond forms and boundaries. What if what seemed isolated was already part of a vaster, elusive movement? CYPHER | Directed by Ruby Gleber | 4:20 | Argentina - Trapped in an unknown facility, a breakdancer attempts to escape the Figures that hunt him. As he tries to satisfy them, he is met with indifference and violence. CYPHER is a surreal psychological exploration of performance as compulsion and art as confinement. What Is the Dark For? | Directed by Derrick Belcham and Daisy Jacobson & Choreography by Daisy Jacobson | 12:00 | United States - In a minimalist dreamscape, a woman navigates a complex tug of war with a tuxedoed apparition, drawing ever closer to a fated confrontation and a question of her own identity. where is my god | Directed by Hyun soo Gavriel Yun | 3:50 | South Korea - At some point, the body disappears. No weight. No boundary. In that state, I search for God. God never appears. Even at the height of it only silence returns. Does the God within me love me? Boys a Bug | Directed by Laurie Lynch & Choreography by Fraser Roach | 6:16 | Czechia Inspired by Franz Kafka's The Metamorphosis, Boys a Bug explores through ballet the grotesque transformation of a man into an insect, tracing his struggle with fear and confusion as he gradually loses his sense of self. Conceived as a true dance film, it places narrative and cinematography at its center, using movement to express the character's psychological descent. WAIL | Cinematography, Editing, and Color by Juan Pablo Salazar & Screenplay by Clara Thierry | 7:10 | Switzerland - WAIL is a poetic exploration of grief and release. The film merges music, dance, and imagery to embody the act of lamentation. Through an expressive visual and sonic language, WAIL invites the viewer into a sensory space where sorrow transforms into motion, and silence becomes sound. your love: ‘sitting' beside me | Directed and Choreographed by Ali Kenner Brodsky | 4:49 | United States - your love: ‘sitting' beside me is the second section of a triptych of short dance films capturing the life cycle of love. "Sitting" is a movement story that explores the nuances and awkwardness of a budding relationship. LIMBES | Directed by Karl Cannone | 5:32 | France - An expressionist dance film opening a window into the dreams and nightmares of a young man. Between paralysis and release, shadow and light, it reflects on collective fears and traumas, and the winding paths toward healing. Vestiges | Directed by Marcus Eriksson & Movement Direction by Medhi Walerski | 4:59 | Canada - Featuring eleven Ballet BC company artists, Vestiges introduces original choreography and movement direction by Medhi Walerski in close collaboration with the dancers, brought to life through Marcus Eriksson's striking cinematic vision and original score. Dash Shaw is a cartoonist and animator. His latest title, Like Swimmers from New York Review Comics, is a fast-paced mystery in lush painted color that delves into loss, calamity, and whether we ever really know the people we love. His previous graphic novel Blurry was named a “graphic novel of the year” by The New York Times, The Washington Post, Forbes and others. He’s also the cartoonist of Discipline, New School, Bottomless Belly Button, BodyWorld and others. He’s written and directed two animated features, most recently the 2021 film Cryptozoo, which won the Sundance Next Innovator Award. He currently lives in Richmond, Virginia.

events.summary: Sitar virtuoso Arjun K. Verma returns to Portland for a special evening of sitar and tabla, with thrilling rhythms and beautiful melodies that invite the listener into the world of North Indian Classical music. Originally developed with the intention of bringing about inner peace, harmony, and unity, this music is also highly virtuosic, and Arjun carries on the tradition of his teacher, Maestro Ali Akbar Khan, in bringing these qualities to modern audiences. Indian classical music has its roots in the sacred, ancient traditions of India, and has evolved into a sophisticated and beautiful art music, now performed and enjoyed by people the world over. Traditionally, it has been passed along from teacher to student in an oral tradition. North Indian Classical Music has a large repertoire of hundreds of traditional melodies, known as raagas, with thousands of songs and instrumental pieces composed in each. One unique aspect of this type of music is that, though it is firmly rooted in a rich, ancient musical tradition with many elements, there is also a tremendous space for each performer to improvise and express his own feelings. Such a performance is authentically unique, spontaneously composed on the spot, and never duplicated again! The improvisatory nature of North Indian Classical Music provides a rich, fresh, and lively performance for listeners to experience.
events.title: Arjun K. Verma

events.summary: Jesse Preis debuts The Raven, a chamber opera composed for three voices and chamber ensemble from Edgar Allan Poe’s poem of the same name, directed by Melory Mirashrafi. In this opera, the narrator (split into two characters to capture the perspective of the Past and the Current at two different stages in life) deals with the loss of a loved one. These complicated, painful, and even terrifying emotions become personified through the character of the Raven. This work is composed with no specific voice types tied to the characters - anyone able to sing the part can and should sing them. This is a groundbreaking composing technique that unties the binds of gendered characters and allows vocalists to portray a character of any gender that is authentic to them and suits their voice. Preis seeks to expand our understanding of vocal writing to go beyond the gendered conventions of soprano, mezzo-soprano, tenor, and bass-baritone, and posits a world where characters are simply written and performed by a wide variety of voices.
events.title: The Raven

events.summary: Written in 1936, this light-hearted comedy has relevance for today in addressing the main theme of finding one’s own way in today’s complex society, while lightly viewing such topics as distrust of government, domestic terrorism and fear of foreign conflicts. “Grandpa” Vanderhof (Robert Lovitz) once worked in the competitive business world. One day, he realized he was unhappy, so he stopped working. Since then, he spends his days catching and raising snakes, watching graduation ceremonies, visiting old friends, and doing whatever else he wants. His daughter Penny (Marilyn Stacey) writes plays simply because a few years ago a typewriter was delivered to the house by accident. His son-in-law Paul Sycamore (Todd Hermanson) spends hours in the basement making illegal fireworks and playing with erector sets. His granddaughter Essie (Bonnie Auguston) sells candy and has been clumsily attempting ballet for over eight years. His grandson-in-law Ed Carmichael (Aiden Brown) plays the xylophone (or tries to) and accidentally distributes Marxist propaganda. Joining this free-for-all are Rheba (Caren Graham), the household cook; her unemployed boyfriend, Donald (Shaun Hennessy); Essie’s opinionated Russian ballet instructor, Mr. Kolenkhov (Mark Schwahn); Olga (Trisha Todd), a Russian Grand Duchess; Gay Wellington (Adrienne Southard), a heavy-drinking actress; Wilbur C. Henderson (Douglas Hout), a forlorn IRS employee; and Mr. De Pinna (Danny Bruno), a deliveryman who arrived 8 years ago and decided to stay. He now helps with the fireworks and dresses in Roman togas to pose for Penny’s portraits. All is somewhat calm until three men from the government (Christopher Sparks, Dan Weiss, and Erik James) visit to investigate Ed’s flyers. In this crazy mix of characters, there is also Alice (Taylor Jean Grady), Penny and Paul’s other daughter and, apparently, the only “normal” family member. She met Tony Kirby (Noah Matthew Rich) at his dad’s Wall Street investment firm, and they’ve fallen in love. Culture shock and fireworks fly when Mr. Kirby (Jeremy Southard) and Mrs. Kirby (Wendy Martel) come to visit. But the message is clear: “Life’s pretty simple if you just relax,” as Grandpa puts it. You Can’t Take It With You is directed by Don Alder. Set design is by Chris Whitten, lighting design is by Demetri Pavlatos, costume design is by Janelle Sutton, prop design is by Allen R. Phillips, the stage manager is Alex Salem, the assistant stage manager is Nat Weinham, and the producer is Steve Knox.

events.summary: Adapted from Agatha Christie’s classic mystery, this immersive production brings the psychological tension of the classic tale into immediate, breath-held proximity. Our story takes place inside a remote seaside mansion after a violent storm strands ten guests and their hosts. When an eerie accusation recorded on a gramophone accuses each of them of wrongdoing, the guests confront secrets, guilt, and suspicion. Trapped by weather and circumstance, alliances form and fracture… old grievances surface, and rationality gives way to intense fear as each new death raises the stakes. At ETP’s production, you’ll find yourself sitting with the characters within the house itself, among the bedrooms, the dining room, and narrow passages. Experience the shifting power dynamics and mounting claustrophobia as if you were part of the action. Hear whispered confrontations up close, overhear private confessions, and feel the silence before the next crisis. Though the environment surrounds you, the audience is strictly non-participatory — as a silent witness, a “fly on the wall,” you will never be directly addressed by the characters, nor asked to participate. What to expect in performance: \- Tension-driven mystery with tightly controlled pacing and sudden shocks. \- Strong emphasis on atmosphere: storm sound design, flickering lantern and candlelight, thunder, and selective blackout moments. \- Intense emotional scenes: accusations, breakdowns, moral reckonings, and desperate attempts to find the culprit. \- Minimalist, realistic set dressing that transforms the performance space into a lived-in island mansion, with audience seating integrated into set locations (chairs, benches, window alcoves). \- No audience interaction; observers remain silent and stationary throughout each performance. Content warnings: Multiple onstage deaths and depictions of violence (staged, non-graphic). Mature themes and dialogue — recommended for ages 13+ About Experience Theatre Project: Experience Theatre Project is an innovative, immersive theater company based in Aloha, Oregon. Unlike traditional theaters with rows of seats and a proscenium stage, ETP crafts imaginative and fully surrounding narratives, drawing inspiration from both original and classic stories. Our specialty lies in presenting these tales in an unconventional, unexpected fashion, surrounding audiences in the world of the play, similar to a haunted house or a Disney experience. Limiting audiences to sixty or fewer ensures an intimate and memorable experience. Ticket link: www.experiencetheatreproject.org
events.title: ETP Presents Agatha Christie's And Then There Were None

events.summary: ⭐️ Single tickets go on sale December 15, but you can reserve your tickets now with a season subscription! ⭐️ December 4, 1956 was the legendary night that Elvis Presley, Jerry Lee Lewis, Carl Perkins, and Johnny Cash came together for one of the greatest jam sessions in history—the night that broken promises, secrets, betrayal and celebrations all came to light. events.summary: Bobby Alu w/ Coloso DuoSoul'd Out Presents: Bobby Alu w/ Coloso Duo Doors: 7:00pm Show: 8:00pm Ages 21+. https://www.bobbyalu.com/ https://colosoband.com/ If you ask Byron Bay's Bobby Alu what his music sounds like, he'll tell you how he hopes it makes you feel: like you have your favourite drink in hand, sipping as the sun sets on a balmy evening that's laden with the promise of adventure. In an ideal world, he'd follow summer around the earth, in his endless quest to nail that feeling in his songs. For Bobby it's all about letting the music decide where it takes you - creatively and physically - and following the threads of curiosity large, small and often strange. It's playing ukulele with old friends at the local market in exchange for a box of vegetables, because how weird is it to improvise along to people buying bananas at 7am on a Tuesday? It's going to Ghana with just a hunch and a WhatsApp number to track down the rhythms that lit up his heart. It's touring the world for five years as Xavier Rudd's percussionist, learning how to be in service to the vibe of a room, and how to make the jump to being an international performer in his own right. It's honouring his Samoan heritage through sharing the stage and releasing an EP with his mother to connect with the language of her homeland. Always, it's about being open to discovery: if you choose music, you choose it all. -------------------------------------- Special Note: Ticket holders for this show receive free admission to Jack London's Burly Q Revue Cabaret after the music! Notes on Seating: Open seating, may be limited or standing room only. First come, first seated. Open dance floor may obscure sightlines.

events.summary: Curated by Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK School and Lisa Jarrett Drawing from the Museum’s collection, this exhibition is co-curated by Lisa Jarrett, an artist, educator, and curator, and the Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK Elementary— a group of 4th and 5th grade curators from KSMoCA. Working from a conversation with notable curators Dr. Lowery Stokes Sims and Dr. Leslie King Hammond, the exhibition engages PAM’s collection in new dialogues shaped by emerging curatorial voices and multigenerational knowledge. From theme and concept development, through work selection, and installation, this community curators project highlights the collaborative nature of curatorial practice and museum work. Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK School \(HTC\) is a KSMoCA project. Students participate directly in shaping exhibitions, positioning them as contributors to the museum, and engaging them as researchers, writers, planners, and curators. Through workshops and field trips, students collaborate with artists, visiting curators, and mentors from Portland State University’s College of the Arts. They research how exhibitions are developed, how artworks are interpreted, and how institutional decisions shape public understanding. Expanded curatorial practice includes visual art, writing, performance, research, publishing, and social practice. Co-founded by Lisa Jarrett and Harrell Fletcher, the project began in 2018 at Harriet Tubman Middle School and continues in its current iteration at Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Elementary School.
events.title: Harriet Tubman Center Museum

events.summary: Inspired by Katherine Ace’s 9 Portraits as the foundational starting point for the exhibition, Nine Women Artists will feature the work of the artists shown in Ace’s portrait painting. All mature artists in their careers and with a significant presence in the Northwest, their work reveals a diverse expression of artistic styles from representation to abstraction. There are rich details in the painting. Most notably on the left hangs Henri Fantin-Latour’s A Studio at Les Batignolles, 1870 \(Musée d’Orsay\). In this painting is a formal gathering of male artists. In response to this painting, Katherine asked her subjects to dress in their studio/work clothes as counterpoint, all marked in their characteristic poses. Other Portland women artists are recognized here through their paintings—a small Sally Haley still life hangs in the background, as well as an Amanda Snyder painting behind Phyllis Yes. And to the far right, we have a glimpse of Lucinda Parker’s very large work. Postcards and newspapers scattered on the floor are the exhibition announcements and reviews highlighting the artists’ works. An epic portrait featuring nine women artists of the Northwest, Ace responded to the lack of self-portraits by women artists in history. From left, the artists are: Laura Ross-Paul, Katherine’s self-portrait seated with phone, Mary Josephson, Judy Cooke, Phyllis Yes, Sharon Bronzan, Shu-Ju Wang, Lucinda Parker, and Sherrie Wolf. All are women artists who have made long careers in Portland. As Ace notes about these women, “They have tenacity, have lived through sexist decades, told they couldn’t really be artists—only fit for sleeping with the professor, expected to subvert themselves to male artist machismo.”
events.title: Nine Women Artists

This class will introduce the fundamental principles of Tai Chi Chaun \(or Taijiquan\) using the Yang Style 24 Posture Form. We will work on posture and body alignment alongside principles of movement and meditation. We will also discuss how Tai Chi blends health, meditation, and martial application. This class is suitable for all levels but will be particularly helpful for beginners of all ages. As the owner of Many Roads Martial Arts Center, her focus is nurturing a supportive and safe learning environment while challenging everyone to keep growing and improving. Jay Twitchell, Instructor Jay has studied various martial arts systems including boxing, wrestling, judo, karate, taekwondo, aikido, hopkido, kumdo, and muay thai kick boxing since he was 10. His lifetime of experience getting kicked, punched, choked, kneed, elbowed, and thrown are invaluable in teaching others how not to be. Balancing his martial studies, Jay has 20 years of experience as a massage therapist and movement specialist, offering him a deep knowledge of the human body and healthy practice. events.summary: Mark your calendars! Join us October 2, 3, and 4th, 2026 for the annual Portland Greek Festival! Enjoy authentic Greek food, traditional dance, music, and more with the whole family. When the first Greek immigrants came to the Northwest in the late 1800s to work in fishing, lumber, railroad and other jobs, they established the Holy Trinity Greek Orthodox Church in southeast Portland. After they moved to a larger church on 32nd and NE Glisan in 1952, they needed to find a way to pay off the mortgage. The ladies decided to help by holding a bazaar featuring their handwork, food, pastries, music, and dances from their homeland. This was the beginning of what is now known as the Portland Greek Festival. After seven decades, the Portland Greek Festival has become one of the largest festivals of its kind, sharing our Greek Orthodox faith and rich culture with over 15,000 guests annually. The festival is an iconic event in the Portland Metropolitan area and has been designated as an Oregon Heritage Tradition by the Oregon Heritage Commission. Each year a portion of proceeds from the festival goes toward worthy philanthropic endeavors in the greater Portland community. Learn more at www.portlandgreekfestival.com
events.title: Portland Greek Festival

events.summary: During WWII, young Japanese Americans \(Nisei\) incarcerated at the Minidoka Relocation Center in Southeast Idaho faced a paradox: fight for a country that had stripped them of their civil liberties, taken away their freedom and placed them and their families behind barbed wire, not because they were the enemy but because they looked like the enemy; or, resist the draft because they and their families had been unconstitutionally and unfairly incarcerated. The Nisei Paradox, a theatrical, multi-media stage reading, tells the story of the young Japanese Americans who chose to resist the draft, fighting injustice with civil disobedience from the confines of Minidoka. 32 of them were prosecuted by the federal government; all but one was found guilty. The stage production was created out of the transcripts of these trials in a collaboration between Chief U.S. Magistrate Judge Ronald E. Bush and attorney Jeff Thomson; all the performers are drawn from the legal community. These young men chose a different type of courage than the many Nisei incarcerees who went to war—they chose to resist, to oppose unfair treatment, to stand up to a stacked legal system, only to lose their freedom for a period longer than the 2-year conscription period, longer than the incarceration camps were open, and longer than the war itself. This program is presented by the Japanese American Museum of Oregon and the Oregon Law Foundation.
events.title: The Nisei Paradox: Japanese American Draft Resisters During World War II

events.summary: Written in 1936, this light-hearted comedy has relevance for today in addressing the main theme of finding one’s own way in today’s complex society, while lightly viewing such topics as distrust of government, domestic terrorism and fear of foreign conflicts. “Grandpa” Vanderhof (Robert Lovitz) once worked in the competitive business world. One day, he realized he was unhappy, so he stopped working. Since then, he spends his days catching and raising snakes, watching graduation ceremonies, visiting old friends, and doing whatever else he wants. His daughter Penny (Marilyn Stacey) writes plays simply because a few years ago a typewriter was delivered to the house by accident. His son-in-law Paul Sycamore (Todd Hermanson) spends hours in the basement making illegal fireworks and playing with erector sets. His granddaughter Essie (Bonnie Auguston) sells candy and has been clumsily attempting ballet for over eight years. His grandson-in-law Ed Carmichael (Aiden Brown) plays the xylophone (or tries to) and accidentally distributes Marxist propaganda. Joining this free-for-all are Rheba (Caren Graham), the household cook; her unemployed boyfriend, Donald (Shaun Hennessy); Essie’s opinionated Russian ballet instructor, Mr. Kolenkhov (Mark Schwahn); Olga (Trisha Todd), a Russian Grand Duchess; Gay Wellington (Adrienne Southard), a heavy-drinking actress; Wilbur C. Henderson (Douglas Hout), a forlorn IRS employee; and Mr. De Pinna (Danny Bruno), a deliveryman who arrived 8 years ago and decided to stay. He now helps with the fireworks and dresses in Roman togas to pose for Penny’s portraits. All is somewhat calm until three men from the government (Christopher Sparks, Dan Weiss, and Erik James) visit to investigate Ed’s flyers. In this crazy mix of characters, there is also Alice (Taylor Jean Grady), Penny and Paul’s other daughter and, apparently, the only “normal” family member. She met Tony Kirby (Noah Matthew Rich) at his dad’s Wall Street investment firm, and they’ve fallen in love. Culture shock and fireworks fly when Mr. Kirby (Jeremy Southard) and Mrs. Kirby (Wendy Martel) come to visit. But the message is clear: “Life’s pretty simple if you just relax,” as Grandpa puts it. You Can’t Take It With You is directed by Don Alder. Set design is by Chris Whitten, lighting design is by Demetri Pavlatos, costume design is by Janelle Sutton, prop design is by Allen R. Phillips, the stage manager is Alex Salem, the assistant stage manager is Nat Weinham, and the producer is Steve Knox.
events.title: You Can't Take It With You

Guisy captura los momentos evanescentes y los inmoviliza en el tiempo para ser queridos y disfrutados durante generaciones, incorporando lo maravilloso y lo mágico de la vida en cada cuadro. THE EXPERIENCE We're all aging. Along the way, we encounter ourselves anew and inhabit the vulnerabilities and freedoms of change. Over the past ten years, we've had the privilege of watching so many filmmakers and dancers in our community grow and evolve, including local artists Suzanne Chi, Carla Mann, and Robert Uehlin. As we reflect on a decade of PDFF, it felt especially meaningful to share their documentary, Still Moving: Dancing Across A Lifetime. The film invites us to think about what it means to keep moving, creating, and dancing as our bodies and lives change. When Suzanne Chi turned 40 during the pandemic, she was forced to confront the question all professional dancers eventually face: should I be done dancing? This feature documentary follows Suzanne and her castmates-five dancers aged 42-65- s they rehearse and perform a new evening-length choreography. In navigating the challenges of aging in an industry that valorizes youth, these dancers offer their own perspectives on how and why they are still moving. Following the film there will be a panel discussion. ON SCREEN: Still Moving Still Moving | Directed by Suzanne Chi, Carla Mann, & Robert Uelin | 39:27 | - This documentary follows Suzanne and her castmates-five dancers aged 42-65 - as they rehearse and perform a new evening-length choreography. In navigating the challenges of aging in an industry that valorizes youth, these dancers offer their own perspectives on how and why they are still moving. ON STAGE: Suzanne Chi, Professor Carla Mann, Rober Uehlin Suzanne Chi is a dancer, producer and curator living in Portland, OR. Performing has taken her around the United States, and to Bulgaria and Germany. She has had the pleasure of working with many Portland based artists and choreographers, and co-directs Muddy Feet Dance with Rachel Slater. Together, Muddy Feet's award winning dance films have been screened all across the world. Professor Carla Mann has been a member of the dance faculty since 1995, teaching beginning through advanced levels of contemporary technique, choreography, improvisation, dance cultural studies and special projects. Her choreographic work includes dance for stage, alternative sites, installation and video. Mann has performed with Oslund\+Co/Dance, tEEth, Bonnie Merrill and Minh Tran & Company among others. Mann was awarded a 2015 Oregon Arts Commission Fellowship and was recently profiled in Stance on Dance. During her 2015-16 sabbatical, Mann will serve as Associate Artistic Director of Heidi Duckler Dance Theatre/Northwest and undertake a new choreographic commission for the Northwest Dance Project. Robert Uehlin is a filmmaker based in Portland, Oregon specializing in the translation of contemporary choreography into the language of film. His work has been screened at the American Dance Festival, The Utah International Screendance Festival, The Sans Souci Festival of Dance Cinema, and across the United States. In 2018, he was selected to receive the inaugural Oregon Dance Film Commission and, the following year, he was named the Hinge Alumni Artist in Residence in West-Central, Minnesota. He has adjudicated for the Portland Dance Film Festival and he is the resident curator of the annual DanceBARN Screendance Festival. events.summary: Jesse Preis debuts The Raven, a chamber opera composed for three voices and chamber ensemble from Edgar Allan Poe’s poem of the same name, directed by Melory Mirashrafi. In this opera, the narrator (split into two characters to capture the perspective of the Past and the Current at two different stages in life) deals with the loss of a loved one. These complicated, painful, and even terrifying emotions become personified through the character of the Raven. This work is composed with no specific voice types tied to the characters - anyone able to sing the part can and should sing them. This is a groundbreaking composing technique that unties the binds of gendered characters and allows vocalists to portray a character of any gender that is authentic to them and suits their voice. Preis seeks to expand our understanding of vocal writing to go beyond the gendered conventions of soprano, mezzo-soprano, tenor, and bass-baritone, and posits a world where characters are simply written and performed by a wide variety of voices.
events.title: The Raven

events.summary: Run Time: 104 min. TICKETS $15 Doors 6:30 p.m.; Event 7 p.m. Select Showtime to Purchase Tickets Click here to learn more about accessibility at the Tomorrow Theater. THE EXPERIENCE We've watched a lot of dance films. For this tenth anniversary, we wanted to revisit a few of the films that have stayed with us. Directors' Picks: A Decade of PDFF is a cohort of nine films from the festival's history that have remained especially meaningful to us. They come from nine countries and span a remarkable range of voices, styles, and stories. Together, these films offer a glimpse into the array of work that has excited and moved us over the years. Please note there is brief nudity throughout this whole program. ON SCREEN: Directors' Picks: 10 Years of PDFF Old Man at the Corner Store, 2023 | Directed by Nadav Heyman and Anabella Casanova & Choreography by Nadav Heyman and Cheryl Mann | 8:10 | United States - An elderly man crosses paths with young neighborhood mischief-makers and dances them through a game of "follow the leader." As they race through the streets, movement becomes their language for exchanging taunts, challenges, and new ways of seeing the world. What I Know So Far, 2022 | Directed by Shawn Fitzgerald Ahern & Choreography by Emilie Leriche | 4:59 | France - A movement-and-words soliloquy that keeps track of small thoughts and fragments of knowledge, shaped as a poetic reminder. Table for one, please., 2024 | Directed and Choreographed by Samantha Shay | 14:10 | Germany & United Kingdom - Emerging from rehearsals for the dance-theater work Life in this House is Over, this short explores the social awkwardness of grief through text, movement, memory, and dramatic vignettes. Inspired by Anton Chekhov, artists connected to Tanztheater Wuppertal Pina Bausch and Teatr ZAR reflect on the blurred boundary between past and future. Dive, 2021 | Directed by Oscar Sansom & Choreography by Sophie Laplane | 13:00 | United Kingdom - Inspired by the visionary work of French artist Yves Klein, Dive immerses Scottish Ballet dancers in a monochrome blue world of empty white space. From stillness, the choreography moves into unexpected complexity, pairing Laplane's distinctive movement with striking, teal-toned cinematography. Second Seed, 2020 | Directed and Choreographed by Amadi "Baye" Washington and Sam "Asa" Pratt | 15:24 | United States - A dance-horror film responding to D. W. Griffith's The Birth of a Nation, Second Seed confronts the white-supremacist mythology and white victimhood embedded in Griffith's film, reframing that history through contemporary Black movement and imagery. TWINS: You Must Be Related!, 2018 | Directed by Varya Rootwood & Choreography by India Gonzalez and Ananda Gonzalez | 3:48 | United States - Twin sisters use tightly synchronized, increasingly frenetic movement to examine the assumptions placed on twins, their shared identity, the pressures of sisterhood, and the desire for individual independence. Your Approval is Not Essential, 2017 | Directed by Leen Michiels & Choreography by Jelena Kostic | 11:49 | Belgium - After a chance encounter in a supermarket unlocks an unexpected passion, an ordinary woman's gray routine gives way to a colorful, whimsical sensory overload. The film explores the liberating, and unruly, pleasures of letting go of inhibition. Aura, 2023 | Directed and Choreographed by Chenglong Tang | 9:49 | China - Two dancers move through precisely structured, opposing configurations, on a black stage and against the open ocean, exploring balance, interdependence, isolation, and the existential questions of who we are and why we are here. It Cries Too Loudly, 2021 | Directed and Choreographed by Dolly Sfeir | 8:28 | Lebanon / United States - Created in response to the 2020 Beirut explosion and its aftermath, this dance film explores the uneasy overlap of joy and tragedy, as well as the emotional distance and divided belonging experienced by a Lebanese American emigré. ON STAGE: Kailee McMurran, Tia Palomino, Jess Evans Kailee McMurran / Festival Director Kailee McMurran is an award-winning dance filmmaker, performer, and founder/director of Portland Dance Film Fest. A former principal with Rainbow Dance Theatre, she co-founded SubRosa Dance Collective and has performed with Do Jump! Extremely Physical Theater since 2011. She also runs Selkie Stationery, a stationery and watercolor studio. Tia Palomino / Director of Operations Tia Palomino is a performer, teacher, and co-founder of Portland Dance Film Fest. She has performed and taught with Royal Caribbean Cruise Lines, Do Jump! Extremely Physical Theater, Polaris Dance Theatre, POV Dance, SubRosa Dance Collective, and A-WOL Dance Collective. She runs Trampoline Town, a circus studio in SW Portland, where she teaches aerial arts, trampoline, and acrobatics. Jess Evans / Director of Communication Jess Evans is a dancer, choreographer, somatic healer, and co-founder of Portland Dance Film Fest. She has created and performed work as a principal with Rainbow Dance Theater, SubRosa Dance Collective, push/FOLD, and as a solo artist. She is a Licensed Massage Therapist and Certified Mindfulness Meditation Teacher. events.summary: Everybody knows that the Devil has all the best tunes. From Robert Johnson selling his soul at the crossroads to the blood-soaked black metal of Norway, Satan has long loomed large over the music world, striking fear into the hearts of the sanctimonious. But nothing that has gone before will prepare you for the arrival of Twin Temple: Los Angeles' one and only purveyors of Satanic Doo-Wop. Devout Satanists and meticulous preservers of rock'n'roll's ancient, timeless spirit, this black-clad and effortlessly stylish duo have created a sound that blends their Satanic ideology with the irresistible sass and melody of classic '50s and '60s rock 'n'roll. The result is "Twin Temple \(Bring You Their Signature Sound...Satanic Doo-Wop\)", a debut album that not only serves to salute the Dark One, but also delivers some of the catchiest and coolest music to emerge from any genre in years. "It's really just a reflection of everything we love," explains vocalist Alexandra James. "We've always loved rock 'n' roll, especially from the golden era of American music, but we're also Satanists and study the Occult. We both practice magick. It was just a crazy idea-- 'Why can't you love Roy Orbison and hail Satan at the same time?' Satanism has been relegated to the metal scene for so long, but we are Satanists and listen to The Platters and Buddy Holly, you know? We love metal too, but this is a reflection of who we are as people. This record was something we wanted to create for ourselves... we were happy to see that it resonated with other people out there, too." Originally released independently by the band and limited to a suitably malevolent 666 vinyl copies, Twin Temple's debut is so beautifully conceived and executed that it sounds like a long, lost classic from the '60s, unearthed in some dusty studio vault. With Alexandra's soulful but siren-like voice and partner Zachary James' dazzling, authentic arrangements, songs like The Devil \(Didn't Make Me Do It\) and I'm Wicked pledge their allegiance to Satan in the most bizarrely accessible and infectious of ways. Bolstered by plenty of analogue hiss and a devotion to old school recording techniques, it's an album that brings the band's unique and enlightened take on Satanism to vivid, vital life. With a Satanic philosophy that prizes individualism, respect, equality and defiance, Twin Temple are intuitively in tune with rock'n'roll's integral outcast culture, even if the fiendishly seditious sound of Alexandra singing enticingly about Sex Magick may make more than few music critics and unsuspecting punters spit their coffee across the room. Ultimately, this transgressive act of musical mischief is as subversive as it gets in this age of societal division, insidious ignorance and empty hostility. Having sold all 666 copies of "Twin Temple \(Bring You Their Signature Sound...Satanic Doo-Wop\)" in just under 4 months to a quickly growing coven of devoted fans, Alexandra and Zachary now find themselves both in demand and intrigued by future possibilities. The album will receive a full release via Rise Above Records, perhaps not the most obvious home for a record that is likely to polarise opinion in the metal world, at least. As far as Twin Templeare concerned, their uniqueness and charm has served them well so far and Rise Above already feels like home. 2019 promises to be a big year for Twin Temple. As the rest of the world is exposed to the extraordinary likes of I Know How To Hex You and Lucifer, My Love, the band will embark on some major touring in support of Uncle Acid & The Deadbeats and Graveyard, with further plans to spread the word of Satan being formulated as we speak. It seems the Devil's best tunes are in safe hands. Hail Twin Temple. Hail Satan!

events.summary: Adapted from Agatha Christie’s classic mystery, this immersive production brings the psychological tension of the classic tale into immediate, breath-held proximity. Our story takes place inside a remote seaside mansion after a violent storm strands ten guests and their hosts. When an eerie accusation recorded on a gramophone accuses each of them of wrongdoing, the guests confront secrets, guilt, and suspicion. Trapped by weather and circumstance, alliances form and fracture… old grievances surface, and rationality gives way to intense fear as each new death raises the stakes. At ETP’s production, you’ll find yourself sitting with the characters within the house itself, among the bedrooms, the dining room, and narrow passages. Experience the shifting power dynamics and mounting claustrophobia as if you were part of the action. Hear whispered confrontations up close, overhear private confessions, and feel the silence before the next crisis. Though the environment surrounds you, the audience is strictly non-participatory — as a silent witness, a “fly on the wall,” you will never be directly addressed by the characters, nor asked to participate. What to expect in performance: \- Tension-driven mystery with tightly controlled pacing and sudden shocks. \- Strong emphasis on atmosphere: storm sound design, flickering lantern and candlelight, thunder, and selective blackout moments. \- Intense emotional scenes: accusations, breakdowns, moral reckonings, and desperate attempts to find the culprit. \- Minimalist, realistic set dressing that transforms the performance space into a lived-in island mansion, with audience seating integrated into set locations (chairs, benches, window alcoves). \- No audience interaction; observers remain silent and stationary throughout each performance. Content warnings: Multiple onstage deaths and depictions of violence (staged, non-graphic). Mature themes and dialogue — recommended for ages 13+ About Experience Theatre Project: Experience Theatre Project is an innovative, immersive theater company based in Aloha, Oregon. Unlike traditional theaters with rows of seats and a proscenium stage, ETP crafts imaginative and fully surrounding narratives, drawing inspiration from both original and classic stories. Our specialty lies in presenting these tales in an unconventional, unexpected fashion, surrounding audiences in the world of the play, similar to a haunted house or a Disney experience. Limiting audiences to sixty or fewer ensures an intimate and memorable experience. Ticket link: www.experiencetheatreproject.org
events.title: ETP Presents Agatha Christie's And Then There Were None

events.summary:
Code & Coffee is an inclusive, informal co-working session: drink your beverage of choice, bring your laptop, and hang out with your peers! Have engaging conversations, or focus on work or projects. This is a great opportunity to learn from others, share your knowledge, and possibly collaborate on side projects, online courses, or even your day-to-day work.

---- Schedule ----

You're welcome to drop in anytime during the event. We understand that everyone may have external commitments and challenges - join us when you can!

We have informal unscheduled introductions - practice your personal elevator pitch, or take things slower to build your confidence.

---- Venue ----

Fly Chai allow us to informally and freely use their space. If within your budget, we'd appreciate your help to sustain our use of the venue, by purchasing something tasty, whether Chai or otherwise.

Find us at tables with a Code&Coffee sign - or a clump of laptop-users!

Wifi and power outlets are available.
Our meeting area should be accessible - please let us know if not.

---- What to expect ----

Smaller events than you may be used to, with a mixed crowd week-to-week. We expect this is likely due to us meeting weekly, at a less central location.

These may result in what you're looking for:
    A smaller, less intimidating, lower pressure, cozy atmosphere.
    A mix of regular and new faces.
    A simpler schedule - every week, same time, same place - that you can drop into when you like.
    Being closer to you than other events.

Whether those are generally or partly to your liking, we hope you'll consider dropping by sometime!

---- Getting to the venue ----

Look for the venue on the meetup Google map, or alternatives like OpenStreetMap.

-- Driving --

There are limited parking spaces on a lot outside the venue (4+1 accessible), with more in the surrounding area.

-- Transit options --

Beaverton Central (Red/Blue MAX), then walk~ 8 minutes

Beaverton Transit Center (Red/Blue MAX, bus, WES) then walk ~11 minutes

For a shorter walk to the venue, take a bus from Beaverton Transit Center (52 to Farmington/Hall, 76 to Watson/Broadway, 57 to Canyon/Watson)

events.summary: The Multnomah Arts Center (MAC) presents A Good Universe Next Door – A redacted past, a precarious present, and an uncertain future, a group exhibition curated by Celeste Noche and Melanie Stevens. On view in the Front & Center Galleries from September 18 through October 17, 2026, the exhibition features new work by four regional artists: Amber Capwell, Ebony Frison, Maryanna Hollomon, and Orlando Almanza. An opening reception will be held Saturday, September 19, from 1–3 p.m., and an artist talk will take place Saturday, October 10 at 2 p.m. Stevens and Noche invited the artists to consider how utopia and dystopia manifest in their lives, and how they interpret these experiences. Through sculpture, photography, printmaking, and painting, the artists offer visions of futures shaped by remembrance, resistance, solidarity, creativity, and care. Ebony Frison approaches utopia and dystopia as “conditions that coexist within the same historical moment.” Working with archival research, printmaking, photography, and artist books, Frison examines how Black histories persist despite erasure, describing utopia as “a practice of rememory—an active engagement with ancestral knowledge, community care, and historical reclamation.” Maryanna Hollomon highlights the aftermath of war for children and the global systems that produce displacement. “A utopia cannot be achieved without working in solidarity with those most oppressed,” she writes. Her work asks viewers to consider militarism’s impact and to imagine new forms of resistance and collective care. Amber Capwell creates sculptural works that envision utopian possibilities through Tarot readings for endangered Pacific Northwest flora and fauna. “These sculptures exist as a reminder to care,” they write. Their work incorporates queer and trans identities as part of an ecological futurism that demands “a utopia existing where we are allowed to live and thrive.” Orlando Almanza imagines futures built on safety, connection, and community. “I dream of a place where my people can have picnics next to the river, to rest, to laugh… and the grandmothers can enjoy their old age, sitting in their rocking chairs on their front porch,” he writes. “Sueño con el día que pueda ver a mi familia reunida, en la tierra que nos vio nacer” (I dream that one day my family can be reunited, in the land that birthed us). The Multnomah Arts Center is located at 7688 SW Capitol Hwy, Portland, OR, 97219. It is open Monday – Thursday 9 a.m. to 9:30 p.m., and Friday – Saturday 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Additional Information: The Multnomah Arts Center is a part of Portland Parks & Recreation. MAC offers programs in a wide range of visual, music, movement, theater, and literary arts at an affordable cost to people of all ages. In addition to this vibrant arts education program, MAC runs a community-based visual arts exhibition program, which includes the MAC Front & Center Galleries. MAC also hosts theatre, music and dance performances, and other special events. The Multnomah Arts Center Association (MACA) is an all-volunteer, 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization that exists to support equity and access to arts education at MAC. MACA provides scholarships, supports community engagements efforts, and provides specialized arts equipment and facility improvements. Their efforts expand opportunities and enhance the experience of students, instructors, and the community at-large. For more information about MAC or MACA, please call 503.823.2787 or visit www.multnomahartscenter.org.
events.title: A Good Universe Next Door

events.summary: The Multnomah Arts Center (MAC) presents A Good Universe Next Door – A redacted past, a precarious present, and an uncertain future, a group exhibition curated by Celeste Noche and Melanie Stevens. On view in the Front & Center Galleries from September 18 through October 17, 2026, the exhibition features new work by four regional artists: Amber Capwell, Ebony Frison, Maryanna Hollomon, and Orlando Almanza. An opening reception will be held Saturday, September 19, from 1–3 p.m., and an artist talk will take place Saturday, October 10 at 2 p.m. Stevens and Noche invited the artists to consider how utopia and dystopia manifest in their lives, and how they interpret these experiences. Through sculpture, photography, printmaking, and painting, the artists offer visions of futures shaped by remembrance, resistance, solidarity, creativity, and care. Ebony Frison approaches utopia and dystopia as “conditions that coexist within the same historical moment.” Working with archival research, printmaking, photography, and artist books, Frison examines how Black histories persist despite erasure, describing utopia as “a practice of rememory—an active engagement with ancestral knowledge, community care, and historical reclamation.” Maryanna Hollomon highlights the aftermath of war for children and the global systems that produce displacement. “A utopia cannot be achieved without working in solidarity with those most oppressed,” she writes. Her work asks viewers to consider militarism’s impact and to imagine new forms of resistance and collective care. Amber Capwell creates sculptural works that envision utopian possibilities through Tarot readings for endangered Pacific Northwest flora and fauna. “These sculptures exist as a reminder to care,” they write. Their work incorporates queer and trans identities as part of an ecological futurism that demands “a utopia existing where we are allowed to live and thrive.” Orlando Almanza imagines futures built on safety, connection, and community. “I dream of a place where my people can have picnics next to the river, to rest, to laugh… and the grandmothers can enjoy their old age, sitting in their rocking chairs on their front porch,” he writes. “Sueño con el día que pueda ver a mi familia reunida, en la tierra que nos vio nacer” (I dream that one day my family can be reunited, in the land that birthed us). The Multnomah Arts Center is located at 7688 SW Capitol Hwy, Portland, OR, 97219. It is open Monday – Thursday 9 a.m. to 9:30 p.m., and Friday – Saturday 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Additional Information: The Multnomah Arts Center is a part of Portland Parks & Recreation. MAC offers programs in a wide range of visual, music, movement, theater, and literary arts at an affordable cost to people of all ages. In addition to this vibrant arts education program, MAC runs a community-based visual arts exhibition program, which includes the MAC Front & Center Galleries. MAC also hosts theatre, music and dance performances, and other special events. The Multnomah Arts Center Association (MACA) is an all-volunteer, 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization that exists to support equity and access to arts education at MAC. MACA provides scholarships, supports community engagements efforts, and provides specialized arts equipment and facility improvements. Their efforts expand opportunities and enhance the experience of students, instructors, and the community at-large. For more information about MAC or MACA, please call 503.823.2787 or visit www.multnomahartscenter.org.
events.title: A Good Universe Next Door

events.summary: Curated by Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK School and Lisa Jarrett Drawing from the Museum’s collection, this exhibition is co-curated by Lisa Jarrett, an artist, educator, and curator, and the Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK Elementary— a group of 4th and 5th grade curators from KSMoCA. Working from a conversation with notable curators Dr. Lowery Stokes Sims and Dr. Leslie King Hammond, the exhibition engages PAM’s collection in new dialogues shaped by emerging curatorial voices and multigenerational knowledge. From theme and concept development, through work selection, and installation, this community curators project highlights the collaborative nature of curatorial practice and museum work. Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK School \(HTC\) is a KSMoCA project. Students participate directly in shaping exhibitions, positioning them as contributors to the museum, and engaging them as researchers, writers, planners, and curators. Through workshops and field trips, students collaborate with artists, visiting curators, and mentors from Portland State University’s College of the Arts. They research how exhibitions are developed, how artworks are interpreted, and how institutional decisions shape public understanding. Expanded curatorial practice includes visual art, writing, performance, research, publishing, and social practice. Co-founded by Lisa Jarrett and Harrell Fletcher, the project began in 2018 at Harriet Tubman Middle School and continues in its current iteration at Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Elementary School.
events.title: Harriet Tubman Center Museum

events.summary: Inspired by Katherine Ace’s 9 Portraits as the foundational starting point for the exhibition, Nine Women Artists will feature the work of the artists shown in Ace’s portrait painting. All mature artists in their careers and with a significant presence in the Northwest, their work reveals a diverse expression of artistic styles from representation to abstraction. There are rich details in the painting. Most notably on the left hangs Henri Fantin-Latour’s A Studio at Les Batignolles, 1870 \(Musée d’Orsay\). In this painting is a formal gathering of male artists. In response to this painting, Katherine asked her subjects to dress in their studio/work clothes as counterpoint, all marked in their characteristic poses. Other Portland women artists are recognized here through their paintings—a small Sally Haley still life hangs in the background, as well as an Amanda Snyder painting behind Phyllis Yes. And to the far right, we have a glimpse of Lucinda Parker’s very large work. Postcards and newspapers scattered on the floor are the exhibition announcements and reviews highlighting the artists’ works. An epic portrait featuring nine women artists of the Northwest, Ace responded to the lack of self-portraits by women artists in history. From left, the artists are: Laura Ross-Paul, Katherine’s self-portrait seated with phone, Mary Josephson, Judy Cooke, Phyllis Yes, Sharon Bronzan, Shu-Ju Wang, Lucinda Parker, and Sherrie Wolf. All are women artists who have made long careers in Portland. As Ace notes about these women, “They have tenacity, have lived through sexist decades, told they couldn’t really be artists—only fit for sleeping with the professor, expected to subvert themselves to male artist machismo.”
events.title: Nine Women Artists

events.summary: A Conversation with Tim Leatherman, Inventor of the Leatherman Multi-Tool Join us on October 6th as we welcome the inventor of the Leatherman multi-tool to Powell's! Tim Leatherman, creator of the Leatherman Pocket Survival Tool and cofounder of the iconic Portland company, presents his inspiring personal story as a practical how-to guide for entrepreneurs, inventors, artists, and creatives of all kinds who want to pursue their own big ideas. On a budget trip to Europe in 1975, Tim started making a list of ideas for what to do with the rest of his life. After months of fixing the plumbing in cheap hotels and toiling on his temperamental Fiat, he added to his list of ideas: “Add pliers to pocketknife.” Little did he know he would spend the following four decades building an iconic American company that would go on to manufacture more than 90 million multi-tools in its Portland, Oregon factory. His latest multi-tool is a book. In The Leatherman Book \(Ballantine\), Tim uses the pieces of his story as tools to help dreamers, entrepreneurs, inventors, and creatives of all kinds build their own big ideas. Each chapter shares valuable insight into how Tim built his invention and his company — and the lessons he’s learned doing it — including: \* You don’t have to be "qualified" to pursue your big idea. \* If you’re serious about your principles, they become your competitive advantage. \* Your most important tool is a willingness to figure things out as you go along. Weaving storytelling, advice, and never-before-seen photos, The Leatherman Book is a visionary and intimate look at a true American icon, meant to inspire and enable dreamers to bring their ideas to life. Leatherman will be joined in conversation by Chris Kornelis, The Leatherman Book co-author, and The Wall Street Journal reporter, and moderated by Bill Monroe, longtime outdoor writer for The Oregonian/OregonLive — and the first journalist to write about the Leatherman multi-tool! Please note: This is a ticketed event. Tickets include admission, as well as one hardcover copy of The Leatherman Book. Books distributed at event. ️: Purchase your book-inclusive ticket: https://www.eventbrite.com/e/a-conversation-with-tim-leatherman-inventor-of-the-leatherman-multi-tool-tickets-1991496445478?aff=oddtdtcreator
events.title: Powell's Presents: Tim Leatherman, Inventor of the Leatherman Multi-Tool - TICKETED EVENT

events.summary: Madeleine Kelson is a Nashville based Americana artist. She pulls from a rich tradition of Folk, Country, and Americana, challenging its boundaries as a queer artist to represent the modern world. Madeleine spent her high school years in Chicago band, The Kelson Twins, playing venues including House of Blues and Thalia Hall, and landing a top Daytrotter Session with Paste Magazine. She later moved to Music City to pursue a solo career. Inspired by artists like Patty Griffin, Jason Isbell, andBrandi Carlile, her dynamic and down-to-earth storytelling and rich vocals are part of why NPR named her one 10 Nashville artists on the rise. Once in Nashville, Madeleine won the 2017 International Bluegrass MusicAssociation’s \(IBMA\) Songwriter Showcase, and in 2018 released her acclaimed solo debut Siren, an introspective five-song EP with clean, melodic vocals backed by elegant countermelodies on violin. Praised by press for its genre-defying, sparse style and emotional richness, Siren earned Kelson comparisons to both Amos Lee and Gillian Welch. In 2022, Madeleine released her debut, self-produced album, While I Was Away, on Olivia Records. Since its release she has gained praise from No Depression, been featured multiple times in NPR, and was a finalist in the prestigious Kerrville New Folk songwriting competition. Her queer country anthem, The Way I Do, became a viral TikTok hit with over 1.7 million views. Madeleine has been featured on Spotify editorial playlists including Queer as Folk, Emerging Americana, and Fresh Finds Folk. Her new EP, Where the Spirit Meets the Muscle, was released in February 2024. “Kelson’s voice is rich and warm” — NPR “I love when an entire record knocks me out and...Madeleine Kelson has done just that.” — WMOT “The Way I Do… is an iconic LGBTQ\+ anthem, and in my opinion, it’s one of the most compelling songs about queer love and pride” — THE BLUEGRASS SITUATION

events.summary: I am Elias Hix. I grew up on a cattle farm in South Carolina. I am shaped by the south's summers of thick heat and hazy air that are soon followed by the cold of harsh and dry winters that leave the sky empty and hollow. Days from those seasons are trapped in my head, with places I will not go anymore, and names that will not leave my lips. When I was 15 I wrote a song called Thinner and then two years later I wrote and produced an album with that song as its title track. This album and the projects that followed are the products of the things I do not speak of anymore and the things I am now too scared to say. So I write them in music, disguised within the imagery and metaphors of the place I grew up in. This is the honest truth of my music and I hope it can help you the way it is helping me. Thank you.
events.title: Elias Hix & Phillip Phillips

events.summary: The Multnomah Arts Center (MAC) presents A Good Universe Next Door – A redacted past, a precarious present, and an uncertain future, a group exhibition curated by Celeste Noche and Melanie Stevens. On view in the Front & Center Galleries from September 18 through October 17, 2026, the exhibition features new work by four regional artists: Amber Capwell, Ebony Frison, Maryanna Hollomon, and Orlando Almanza. An opening reception will be held Saturday, September 19, from 1–3 p.m., and an artist talk will take place Saturday, October 10 at 2 p.m. Stevens and Noche invited the artists to consider how utopia and dystopia manifest in their lives, and how they interpret these experiences. Through sculpture, photography, printmaking, and painting, the artists offer visions of futures shaped by remembrance, resistance, solidarity, creativity, and care. Ebony Frison approaches utopia and dystopia as “conditions that coexist within the same historical moment.” Working with archival research, printmaking, photography, and artist books, Frison examines how Black histories persist despite erasure, describing utopia as “a practice of rememory—an active engagement with ancestral knowledge, community care, and historical reclamation.” Maryanna Hollomon highlights the aftermath of war for children and the global systems that produce displacement. “A utopia cannot be achieved without working in solidarity with those most oppressed,” she writes. Her work asks viewers to consider militarism’s impact and to imagine new forms of resistance and collective care. Amber Capwell creates sculptural works that envision utopian possibilities through Tarot readings for endangered Pacific Northwest flora and fauna. “These sculptures exist as a reminder to care,” they write. Their work incorporates queer and trans identities as part of an ecological futurism that demands “a utopia existing where we are allowed to live and thrive.” Orlando Almanza imagines futures built on safety, connection, and community. “I dream of a place where my people can have picnics next to the river, to rest, to laugh… and the grandmothers can enjoy their old age, sitting in their rocking chairs on their front porch,” he writes. “Sueño con el día que pueda ver a mi familia reunida, en la tierra que nos vio nacer” (I dream that one day my family can be reunited, in the land that birthed us). The Multnomah Arts Center is located at 7688 SW Capitol Hwy, Portland, OR, 97219. It is open Monday – Thursday 9 a.m. to 9:30 p.m., and Friday – Saturday 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Additional Information: The Multnomah Arts Center is a part of Portland Parks & Recreation. MAC offers programs in a wide range of visual, music, movement, theater, and literary arts at an affordable cost to people of all ages. In addition to this vibrant arts education program, MAC runs a community-based visual arts exhibition program, which includes the MAC Front & Center Galleries. MAC also hosts theatre, music and dance performances, and other special events. The Multnomah Arts Center Association (MACA) is an all-volunteer, 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization that exists to support equity and access to arts education at MAC. MACA provides scholarships, supports community engagements efforts, and provides specialized arts equipment and facility improvements. Their efforts expand opportunities and enhance the experience of students, instructors, and the community at-large. For more information about MAC or MACA, please call 503.823.2787 or visit www.multnomahartscenter.org.
events.title: A Good Universe Next Door

Working from a conversation with notable curators Dr. Lowery Stokes Sims and Dr. Leslie King Hammond, the exhibition engages PAM’s collection in new dialogues shaped by emerging curatorial voices and multigenerational knowledge. From theme and concept development, through work selection, and installation, this community curators project highlights the collaborative nature of curatorial practice and museum work. Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK School \(HTC\) is a KSMoCA project. Students participate directly in shaping exhibitions, positioning them as contributors to the museum, and engaging them as researchers, writers, planners, and curators. Through workshops and field trips, students collaborate with artists, visiting curators, and mentors from Portland State University’s College of the Arts. They research how exhibitions are developed, how artworks are interpreted, and how institutional decisions shape public understanding. Expanded curatorial practice includes visual art, writing, performance, research, publishing, and social practice. Co-founded by Lisa Jarrett and Harrell Fletcher, the project began in 2018 at Harriet Tubman Middle School and continues in its current iteration at Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Elementary School.

events.summary: Inspired by Katherine Ace’s 9 Portraits as the foundational starting point for the exhibition, Nine Women Artists will feature the work of the artists shown in Ace’s portrait painting. All mature artists in their careers and with a significant presence in the Northwest, their work reveals a diverse expression of artistic styles from representation to abstraction. There are rich details in the painting. Most notably on the left hangs Henri Fantin-Latour’s A Studio at Les Batignolles, 1870 \(Musée d’Orsay\). In this painting is a formal gathering of male artists. In response to this painting, Katherine asked her subjects to dress in their studio/work clothes as counterpoint, all marked in their characteristic poses. Other Portland women artists are recognized here through their paintings—a small Sally Haley still life hangs in the background, as well as an Amanda Snyder painting behind Phyllis Yes. And to the far right, we have a glimpse of Lucinda Parker’s very large work. Postcards and newspapers scattered on the floor are the exhibition announcements and reviews highlighting the artists’ works. An epic portrait featuring nine women artists of the Northwest, Ace responded to the lack of self-portraits by women artists in history. From left, the artists are: Laura Ross-Paul, Katherine’s self-portrait seated with phone, Mary Josephson, Judy Cooke, Phyllis Yes, Sharon Bronzan, Shu-Ju Wang, Lucinda Parker, and Sherrie Wolf. All are women artists who have made long careers in Portland. As Ace notes about these women, “They have tenacity, have lived through sexist decades, told they couldn’t really be artists—only fit for sleeping with the professor, expected to subvert themselves to male artist machismo.”
events.title: Nine Women Artists

events.summary: Chefas Projects is pleased to present Mercurial, a new solo exhibition by sculptural artist Dan Lam, on view September 18 through October 17, 2026. Bringing together more than twenty new works, the exhibition introduces a heightened metallic sensibility to Lam’s singular sculptural language, with surfaces that suggest chrome, liquid metal, and something less readily identifiable-objects caught somewhere between matter and mutation. Known for sculptures that occupy an uncanny space between the organic and the artificial, Lam approaches form as something fluid, seductive, and alive. In Mercurial, this sensibility takes on a distinctly reflective character. Metallic hues course across the surfaces of the works, emphasizing their bulbous contours, dripping edges, and seemingly unstable forms. Chrome-like finishes catch and distort their surroundings, allowing the sculptures to shift with changes in light, perspective, and proximity. The works appear to ooze, pool, drip, and swell. Their surfaces suggest viscosity while their forms remain resolutely sculptural, creating an intriguing contradiction between solidity and liquidity. They seem less like objects that have been made than organisms in the midst of becoming - alien, tactile, and strangely familiar. This tension is fundamental to Lam’s practice. Her sculptures consistently operate between opposing states: attraction and repulsion, organic and inanimate, soft and hard, seriousness and play. Rather than resolving these contradictions, Lam uses them as points of departure. The resulting forms possess an uncanny immediacy, inviting viewers to move closer even as their unfamiliarity introduces a note of hesitation. In Mercurial, the reflective surfaces intensify this exchange between object and viewer. The sculptures absorb fragments of their environments and return them altered, making the surrounding space part of the work. What initially reads as an autonomous object becomes something more relational-a form that changes depending on where it is encountered and how it is seen. Despite their otherworldly appearance, Lam’s sculptures remain remarkably approachable. Playfulness is central to their charge. The works resist the distance sometimes associated with contemporary sculpture, instead engaging the viewer through color, surface, scale, and a visceral sense of recognition. They are strange without being alienating; experimental without abandoning the pleasures of looking. The title Mercurial evokes both the mutable nature of the works and their affinity with mercury: a substance defined by its fluidity, reflectivity, and ability to transform its appearance in relation to its surroundings. Here, Lam translates those qualities into sculptural form. Her objects appear perpetually in motion, suspended between states, as though their final form has not yet been decided. Across more than twenty new sculptures, Mercurial expands Lam’s investigation of the space between the familiar and the unknown. The works activate the imagination through an intuitive visual language - one based not on representation but on sensation. Their exaggerated forms, seductive surfaces, and ambiguous materiality encourage viewers to project, imagine, and participate. In Lam’s hands, sculpture becomes less a fixed thing than an encounter: part organism, part object, part fantasy. Mercurial embraces that instability, presenting a body of work that is at once polished and unruly, seductive and strange, playful and profound.
events.title: DAN LAM | MERCURIAL

events.summary: Chefas Projects is pleased to present Galvanized, the first solo exhibition at the gallery by Portland artist Bobby Adams. On view September 18 through October 17, the exhibition brings together seven new gradient paintings that extend Adams’s ongoing investigation into color, movement, precision, and reduction. Working with hard edges and meticulously calibrated color transitions, Adams constructs paintings that appear at once exacting and elusive. Color becomes both subject and structure: gradients shift across the surface with a measured sense of movement, while simplified compositions heighten the perceptual effects of scale, saturation, and transition. The paintings inhabit a productive space between the mechanical and the handmade, where precision does not eliminate the presence of the artist but makes it more apparent. Adams’s approach is informed by a background outside of traditional art-making. Before turning to painting in 2017, he worked in product development and ran a clothing line for eight years. That experience with materials, systems, color, and visual identity remains embedded in his practice. His paintings share an affinity with the economy and immediacy of graphic design while resisting its fixedness; seemingly simple arrangements become dynamic through subtle shifts in color and proportion. The title Galvanized gestures toward a central tension within the work: the desire to achieve a polished, controlled image alongside the inevitable irregularities of its making. Adams’s paintings are rigorously constructed, but they are not anonymous. Their surfaces hold the evidence of decisions, adjustments, and the physical act of painting. Running through the exhibition is Adams’s longstanding relationship to NASCAR, a significant influence on his upbringing and visual sensibility. The sport’s saturated palettes, speed, spectacle, and graphic intensity provide an unexpected point of departure for paintings that are otherwise characterized by restraint. In California Poppy, this connection is particularly pronounced. Its color relationships carry the visual charge of racing culture while being distilled through Adams’s pared-down formal language. The result is a body of work in which speed is suggested rather than depicted, and where movement emerges from the most economical means. Adams takes visual cues associated with motion, competition, and spectacle and subjects them to the slower, more deliberate logic of abstraction. Galvanized marks an important step in Adams’s relationship with the gallery, following his inclusion in multiple group exhibitions and establishing a sustained presentation of his practice through a focused body of new work.
events.title: BOBBY ADAMS | GALVANIZED

events.summary:
#### Assistive Tech User Research

Join us as Cindy Merrill shares her work making technology more accessible to people with disabilities. Cindy conducts remote moderated research with people who use assistive technology, including screen readers and screen magnifiers. In this presentation, she'll discuss real-world insights from her research and share proven best practices for planning and conducting effective user research with people who rely on these essential tools.

This event is co-hosted by [CHIFOO](https://chifoo.org/) (pronounced ‘ky – FOO’), the Computer Human Interaction Forum of Oregon, and [PDX A11Y UX](https://pdxa11yux.org/), the Portland Accessibility & UX Meetup.

#### Bio

[Cindy Merrill](https://www.linkedin.com/in/cindymerrill/) is a Lead UX Researcher at Pluribus Digital, a consulting firm specializing in modern digital experiences for the federal government. With more than 20 years of experience in user research across government and industry, she is passionate about making technology more accessible and easier to use. She has conducted numerous research studies on websites, consumer products, and automotive systems while working at Intel, Jaguar Land Rover, Cvent, and various consulting firms.

#### Event is in person and online

We are in person at the Multnomah County Central Library (Large Community Room 1A) and online via Zoom for remote participation (Zoom link will be posted a few days before event). Introduction starts at 6:00 pm, and we need to leave the room by 7:45pm.

#### Accommodation requests

If you have any accommodation requests, don’t hesitate to contact us before the event to discuss.
events.title: Assistive Tech User Research with Cindy Merrill (Hybrid) - CHIFOO / PDX A11Y UX
