events.summary: About the Event Feng E first stunned the world at just ten years old when his mesmerizing ukulele rendition of Tommy Emmanuel’s Classical Gas went viral. Almost overnight, the young prodigy became an international sensation—appearing twice on The Ellen DeGeneres Show and captivating millions more on Asia’s Got Talent and America’s Got Talent. Since those early viral days, Feng E has evolved into one of the most electrifying young artists in the global ukulele scene. His dazzling performances have graced stages across Singapore, Malaysia, Japan, China, and Hawaii, earning him international awards and headline slots. His groundbreaking 2024 U.S. West Coast tour wowed audiences with show-stopping sets at the Los Angeles International Ukulele Festival, alongside national TV and radio appearances. In 2025, he headlined the Denver International Ukulele Festival and was an official showcase artist and panelist for the New Orleans Folk Alliance conference. He went on to packed houses up and down the East Coast, including the Cutting Room in New York City With nearly one million YouTube subscribers and countless millions of views, Feng E continues to push boundaries and redefine what the ukulele can do. In 2025, he and his band Resonance Effect captured the top prize at Taiwan’s Taoyuan Iron Rose Hot Sound Awards—their version of Idol. Now, this teenage virtuoso returns to U.S. stages, ready to captivate audiences once again. Experience the energy, emotion, and pure joy of an artist who’s redefining a generation of music. fengemusic.com

events.summary: Hello from in here to all you out there. Fruit Bats’ eighth LP opens with this invocation, this call from an isolated vocal room to your headphones somewhere out in the world. It’s a beckoning for your trust and attention, but also an assurance in lonely times—a distillation of melancholy wrapped in a danceable waltz. “The Pet Parade,” the title track to Fruit Bats’ newest album, might be a surprising opening track for longtime fans of Eric D. Johnson’s beloved indie folk-rock project.The six-and-a-half-minute tone poem smolders and drones over just two chords, inspired by the strange and silly community events that he saw growing up outside of Chicago, in La Grange, Illinois, in which people dressed up and showed off their pets. Decades later, The Pet Parade emerges in troubled times, living within what Johnson refers to as the beauty and absurdity of existence. At times upbeat and reassuring \(“Eagles Below Us”\) and at times quietly contemplative \(“On the Avalon Stairs”\), The Pet Parade marks a milestone for Johnson, who celebrates 20 years of Fruit Bats in 2021. In some ways still a cult band, in other ways a time-tested act, Fruit Bats has consistently earned enough small victories to carve out a career in a notoriously fickle scene.

events.summary: The Multnomah Arts Center (MAC) presents A Good Universe Next Door – A redacted past, a precarious present, and an uncertain future, a group exhibition curated by Celeste Noche and Melanie Stevens. On view in the Front & Center Galleries from September 18 through October 17, 2026, the exhibition features new work by four regional artists: Amber Capwell, Ebony Frison, Maryanna Hollomon, and Orlando Almanza. An opening reception will be held Saturday, September 19, from 1–3 p.m., and an artist talk will take place Saturday, October 10 at 2 p.m. Stevens and Noche invited the artists to consider how utopia and dystopia manifest in their lives, and how they interpret these experiences. Through sculpture, photography, printmaking, and painting, the artists offer visions of futures shaped by remembrance, resistance, solidarity, creativity, and care. Ebony Frison approaches utopia and dystopia as “conditions that coexist within the same historical moment.” Working with archival research, printmaking, photography, and artist books, Frison examines how Black histories persist despite erasure, describing utopia as “a practice of rememory—an active engagement with ancestral knowledge, community care, and historical reclamation.” Maryanna Hollomon highlights the aftermath of war for children and the global systems that produce displacement. “A utopia cannot be achieved without working in solidarity with those most oppressed,” she writes. Her work asks viewers to consider militarism’s impact and to imagine new forms of resistance and collective care. Amber Capwell creates sculptural works that envision utopian possibilities through Tarot readings for endangered Pacific Northwest flora and fauna. “These sculptures exist as a reminder to care,” they write. Their work incorporates queer and trans identities as part of an ecological futurism that demands “a utopia existing where we are allowed to live and thrive.” Orlando Almanza imagines futures built on safety, connection, and community. “I dream of a place where my people can have picnics next to the river, to rest, to laugh… and the grandmothers can enjoy their old age, sitting in their rocking chairs on their front porch,” he writes. “Sueño con el día que pueda ver a mi familia reunida, en la tierra que nos vio nacer” (I dream that one day my family can be reunited, in the land that birthed us). The Multnomah Arts Center is located at 7688 SW Capitol Hwy, Portland, OR, 97219. It is open Monday – Thursday 9 a.m. to 9:30 p.m., and Friday – Saturday 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Additional Information: The Multnomah Arts Center is a part of Portland Parks & Recreation. MAC offers programs in a wide range of visual, music, movement, theater, and literary arts at an affordable cost to people of all ages. In addition to this vibrant arts education program, MAC runs a community-based visual arts exhibition program, which includes the MAC Front & Center Galleries. MAC also hosts theatre, music and dance performances, and other special events. The Multnomah Arts Center Association (MACA) is an all-volunteer, 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization that exists to support equity and access to arts education at MAC. MACA provides scholarships, supports community engagements efforts, and provides specialized arts equipment and facility improvements. Their efforts expand opportunities and enhance the experience of students, instructors, and the community at-large. For more information about MAC or MACA, please call 503.823.2787 or visit www.multnomahartscenter.org.
events.title: A Good Universe Next Door

events.summary: Curated by Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK School and Lisa Jarrett Drawing from the Museum’s collection, this exhibition is co-curated by Lisa Jarrett, an artist, educator, and curator, and the Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK Elementary— a group of 4th and 5th grade curators from KSMoCA. Working from a conversation with notable curators Dr. Lowery Stokes Sims and Dr. Leslie King Hammond, the exhibition engages PAM’s collection in new dialogues shaped by emerging curatorial voices and multigenerational knowledge. From theme and concept development, through work selection, and installation, this community curators project highlights the collaborative nature of curatorial practice and museum work. Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK School \(HTC\) is a KSMoCA project. Students participate directly in shaping exhibitions, positioning them as contributors to the museum, and engaging them as researchers, writers, planners, and curators. Through workshops and field trips, students collaborate with artists, visiting curators, and mentors from Portland State University’s College of the Arts. They research how exhibitions are developed, how artworks are interpreted, and how institutional decisions shape public understanding. Expanded curatorial practice includes visual art, writing, performance, research, publishing, and social practice. Co-founded by Lisa Jarrett and Harrell Fletcher, the project began in 2018 at Harriet Tubman Middle School and continues in its current iteration at Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Elementary School.

events.summary: Inspired by Katherine Ace’s 9 Portraits as the foundational starting point for the exhibition, Nine Women Artists will feature the work of the artists shown in Ace’s portrait painting. All mature artists in their careers and with a significant presence in the Northwest, their work reveals a diverse expression of artistic styles from representation to abstraction. There are rich details in the painting. Most notably on the left hangs Henri Fantin-Latour’s A Studio at Les Batignolles, 1870 \(Musée d’Orsay\). In this painting is a formal gathering of male artists. In response to this painting, Katherine asked her subjects to dress in their studio/work clothes as counterpoint, all marked in their characteristic poses. Other Portland women artists are recognized here through their paintings—a small Sally Haley still life hangs in the background, as well as an Amanda Snyder painting behind Phyllis Yes. And to the far right, we have a glimpse of Lucinda Parker’s very large work. Postcards and newspapers scattered on the floor are the exhibition announcements and reviews highlighting the artists’ works. An epic portrait featuring nine women artists of the Northwest, Ace responded to the lack of self-portraits by women artists in history. From left, the artists are: Laura Ross-Paul, Katherine’s self-portrait seated with phone, Mary Josephson, Judy Cooke, Phyllis Yes, Sharon Bronzan, Shu-Ju Wang, Lucinda Parker, and Sherrie Wolf. All are women artists who have made long careers in Portland. As Ace notes about these women, “They have tenacity, have lived through sexist decades, told they couldn’t really be artists—only fit for sleeping with the professor, expected to subvert themselves to male artist machismo.”
events.title: Nine Women Artists

events.summary: Chefas Projects is pleased to present Mercurial, a new solo exhibition by sculptural artist Dan Lam, on view September 18 through October 17, 2026. Bringing together more than twenty new works, the exhibition introduces a heightened metallic sensibility to Lam’s singular sculptural language, with surfaces that suggest chrome, liquid metal, and something less readily identifiable-objects caught somewhere between matter and mutation. Known for sculptures that occupy an uncanny space between the organic and the artificial, Lam approaches form as something fluid, seductive, and alive. In Mercurial, this sensibility takes on a distinctly reflective character. Metallic hues course across the surfaces of the works, emphasizing their bulbous contours, dripping edges, and seemingly unstable forms. Chrome-like finishes catch and distort their surroundings, allowing the sculptures to shift with changes in light, perspective, and proximity. The works appear to ooze, pool, drip, and swell. Their surfaces suggest viscosity while their forms remain resolutely sculptural, creating an intriguing contradiction between solidity and liquidity. They seem less like objects that have been made than organisms in the midst of becoming - alien, tactile, and strangely familiar. This tension is fundamental to Lam’s practice. Her sculptures consistently operate between opposing states: attraction and repulsion, organic and inanimate, soft and hard, seriousness and play. Rather than resolving these contradictions, Lam uses them as points of departure. The resulting forms possess an uncanny immediacy, inviting viewers to move closer even as their unfamiliarity introduces a note of hesitation. In Mercurial, the reflective surfaces intensify this exchange between object and viewer. The sculptures absorb fragments of their environments and return them altered, making the surrounding space part of the work. What initially reads as an autonomous object becomes something more relational-a form that changes depending on where it is encountered and how it is seen. Despite their otherworldly appearance, Lam’s sculptures remain remarkably approachable. Playfulness is central to their charge. The works resist the distance sometimes associated with contemporary sculpture, instead engaging the viewer through color, surface, scale, and a visceral sense of recognition. They are strange without being alienating; experimental without abandoning the pleasures of looking. The title Mercurial evokes both the mutable nature of the works and their affinity with mercury: a substance defined by its fluidity, reflectivity, and ability to transform its appearance in relation to its surroundings. Here, Lam translates those qualities into sculptural form. Her objects appear perpetually in motion, suspended between states, as though their final form has not yet been decided. Across more than twenty new sculptures, Mercurial expands Lam’s investigation of the space between the familiar and the unknown. The works activate the imagination through an intuitive visual language - one based not on representation but on sensation. Their exaggerated forms, seductive surfaces, and ambiguous materiality encourage viewers to project, imagine, and participate. In Lam’s hands, sculpture becomes less a fixed thing than an encounter: part organism, part object, part fantasy. Mercurial embraces that instability, presenting a body of work that is at once polished and unruly, seductive and strange, playful and profound.
events.title: DAN LAM | MERCURIAL

events.summary: Chefas Projects is pleased to present Galvanized, the first solo exhibition at the gallery by Portland artist Bobby Adams. On view September 18 through October 17, the exhibition brings together seven new gradient paintings that extend Adams’s ongoing investigation into color, movement, precision, and reduction. Working with hard edges and meticulously calibrated color transitions, Adams constructs paintings that appear at once exacting and elusive. Color becomes both subject and structure: gradients shift across the surface with a measured sense of movement, while simplified compositions heighten the perceptual effects of scale, saturation, and transition. The paintings inhabit a productive space between the mechanical and the handmade, where precision does not eliminate the presence of the artist but makes it more apparent. Adams’s approach is informed by a background outside of traditional art-making. Before turning to painting in 2017, he worked in product development and ran a clothing line for eight years. That experience with materials, systems, color, and visual identity remains embedded in his practice. His paintings share an affinity with the economy and immediacy of graphic design while resisting its fixedness; seemingly simple arrangements become dynamic through subtle shifts in color and proportion. The title Galvanized gestures toward a central tension within the work: the desire to achieve a polished, controlled image alongside the inevitable irregularities of its making. Adams’s paintings are rigorously constructed, but they are not anonymous. Their surfaces hold the evidence of decisions, adjustments, and the physical act of painting. Running through the exhibition is Adams’s longstanding relationship to NASCAR, a significant influence on his upbringing and visual sensibility. The sport’s saturated palettes, speed, spectacle, and graphic intensity provide an unexpected point of departure for paintings that are otherwise characterized by restraint. In California Poppy, this connection is particularly pronounced. Its color relationships carry the visual charge of racing culture while being distilled through Adams’s pared-down formal language. The result is a body of work in which speed is suggested rather than depicted, and where movement emerges from the most economical means. Adams takes visual cues associated with motion, competition, and spectacle and subjects them to the slower, more deliberate logic of abstraction. Galvanized marks an important step in Adams’s relationship with the gallery, following his inclusion in multiple group exhibitions and establishing a sustained presentation of his practice through a focused body of new work.
events.title: BOBBY ADAMS | GALVANIZED

events.summary: Kenth Kvien and Marcus Nordli, better known as Da Tweekaz, are a Norwegian duo celebrated worldwide as one of the biggest Hardstyle acts. With their uplifting energy, infectious stage presence and unique sound, they’ve become a one-of-a-kind act that electrifies every crowd they encounter. Whether behind the decks or raving in the front with their fans, you can always count on them to bring the party to life. From intimate clubs to massive festivals, their global impact is undeniable. With hundreds of millions of streams, they’ve collaborated with some of the biggest names in dance music such as Timmy Trumpet, R3hab, W&W, and fellow Norwegian superstar Alan Walker, whose track 'On My Way' they famously remixed. Their own iconic anthems like Jägermeister, How Far I’ll Go and I Want It All have become staples in Hardstyle culture and beyond. During the 2020 pandemic Da Tweekaz launched Tweeka TV, a livestream show that quickly became a worldwide phenomenon. With up to 15,000 weekly viewers, sunglasses on, Jägermeister flowing and a lineup of special guests, the duo stayed connected with fans when the world needed it most. Even after live events returned, the demand for Tweeka TV was so high that they continue to stream regularly to this day despite the touring and they even recently celebrated the 100th episode. On stage, Da Tweekaz are a true powerhouse, performing at the biggest festivals and mainstages around the world. They’ve rocked the Tomorrowland Mainstage four times, brought their energy to the Mainstages of Tomorrowland Winter and Tomorrowland Brasil and delivered iconic hostings at Tomorrowland itself. Their global footprint also includes Ultra Australia, Ultra Taiwan, Ultra Miami, EDC Korea, World Club Dome, Reverze, Defqon.1, EDC Las Vegas and many more. With their relentless passion and unmatched energy, Da Tweekaz continue to spread joy and Hardstyle around the globe. From the studio to the stage, this duo is unstoppable — and wherever they go, you can be sure the party follows.

events.summary: Written in 1936, this light-hearted comedy has relevance for today in addressing the main theme of finding one’s own way in today’s complex society, while lightly viewing such topics as distrust of government, domestic terrorism and fear of foreign conflicts. “Grandpa” Vanderhof (Robert Lovitz) once worked in the competitive business world. One day, he realized he was unhappy, so he stopped working. Since then, he spends his days catching and raising snakes, watching graduation ceremonies, visiting old friends, and doing whatever else he wants. His daughter Penny (Marilyn Stacey) writes plays simply because a few years ago a typewriter was delivered to the house by accident. His son-in-law Paul Sycamore (Todd Hermanson) spends hours in the basement making illegal fireworks and playing with erector sets. His granddaughter Essie (Bonnie Auguston) sells candy and has been clumsily attempting ballet for over eight years. His grandson-in-law Ed Carmichael (Aiden Brown) plays the xylophone (or tries to) and accidentally distributes Marxist propaganda. Joining this free-for-all are Rheba (Caren Graham), the household cook; her unemployed boyfriend, Donald (Shaun Hennessy); Essie’s opinionated Russian ballet instructor, Mr. Kolenkhov (Mark Schwahn); Olga (Trisha Todd), a Russian Grand Duchess; Gay Wellington (Adrienne Southard), a heavy-drinking actress; Wilbur C. Henderson (Douglas Hout), a forlorn IRS employee; and Mr. De Pinna (Danny Bruno), a deliveryman who arrived 8 years ago and decided to stay. He now helps with the fireworks and dresses in Roman togas to pose for Penny’s portraits. All is somewhat calm until three men from the government (Christopher Sparks, Dan Weiss, and Erik James) visit to investigate Ed’s flyers. In this crazy mix of characters, there is also Alice (Taylor Jean Grady), Penny and Paul’s other daughter and, apparently, the only “normal” family member. She met Tony Kirby (Noah Matthew Rich) at his dad’s Wall Street investment firm, and they’ve fallen in love. Culture shock and fireworks fly when Mr. Kirby (Jeremy Southard) and Mrs. Kirby (Wendy Martel) come to visit. But the message is clear: “Life’s pretty simple if you just relax,” as Grandpa puts it. You Can’t Take It With You is directed by Don Alder. Set design is by Chris Whitten, lighting design is by Demetri Pavlatos, costume design is by Janelle Sutton, prop design is by Allen R. Phillips, the stage manager is Alex Salem, the assistant stage manager is Nat Weinham, and the producer is Steve Knox.
events.title: You Can't Take It With You

events.summary: Glass. Kill. Bluebeard. Imp. is a collection of four short, surreal plays by acclaimed English playwright, Caryl Churchill. Premiering at London's Royal Court Theatre in 2019, these darkly imaginative works weave together myth, fairy tale, and contemporary horror. Moving between collective voices and intimate encounters, Churchill explores violence, power, desire, and the stories we tell to make sense of a fractured world. By turns funny, haunting, and unsettling, the plays invite audiences into a landscape where the familiar becomes strange and ancient myths reveal modern anxieties without explanation or comfort. A girl made of glass. Gods and murders. A serial killer's friends. And a secret in a bottle.​ Four short plays by Caryl Churchill Directed by Samantha Van Der Merwe​October 10th - November 7th 2026

events.summary: The Multnomah Arts Center (MAC) presents A Good Universe Next Door – A redacted past, a precarious present, and an uncertain future, a group exhibition curated by Celeste Noche and Melanie Stevens. On view in the Front & Center Galleries from September 18 through October 17, 2026, the exhibition features new work by four regional artists: Amber Capwell, Ebony Frison, Maryanna Hollomon, and Orlando Almanza. An opening reception will be held Saturday, September 19, from 1–3 p.m., and an artist talk will take place Saturday, October 10 at 2 p.m. Stevens and Noche invited the artists to consider how utopia and dystopia manifest in their lives, and how they interpret these experiences. Through sculpture, photography, printmaking, and painting, the artists offer visions of futures shaped by remembrance, resistance, solidarity, creativity, and care. Ebony Frison approaches utopia and dystopia as “conditions that coexist within the same historical moment.” Working with archival research, printmaking, photography, and artist books, Frison examines how Black histories persist despite erasure, describing utopia as “a practice of rememory—an active engagement with ancestral knowledge, community care, and historical reclamation.” Maryanna Hollomon highlights the aftermath of war for children and the global systems that produce displacement. “A utopia cannot be achieved without working in solidarity with those most oppressed,” she writes. Her work asks viewers to consider militarism’s impact and to imagine new forms of resistance and collective care. Amber Capwell creates sculptural works that envision utopian possibilities through Tarot readings for endangered Pacific Northwest flora and fauna. “These sculptures exist as a reminder to care,” they write. Their work incorporates queer and trans identities as part of an ecological futurism that demands “a utopia existing where we are allowed to live and thrive.” Orlando Almanza imagines futures built on safety, connection, and community. “I dream of a place where my people can have picnics next to the river, to rest, to laugh… and the grandmothers can enjoy their old age, sitting in their rocking chairs on their front porch,” he writes. “Sueño con el día que pueda ver a mi familia reunida, en la tierra que nos vio nacer” (I dream that one day my family can be reunited, in the land that birthed us). The Multnomah Arts Center is located at 7688 SW Capitol Hwy, Portland, OR, 97219. It is open Monday – Thursday 9 a.m. to 9:30 p.m., and Friday – Saturday 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Additional Information: The Multnomah Arts Center is a part of Portland Parks & Recreation. MAC offers programs in a wide range of visual, music, movement, theater, and literary arts at an affordable cost to people of all ages. In addition to this vibrant arts education program, MAC runs a community-based visual arts exhibition program, which includes the MAC Front & Center Galleries. MAC also hosts theatre, music and dance performances, and other special events. The Multnomah Arts Center Association (MACA) is an all-volunteer, 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization that exists to support equity and access to arts education at MAC. MACA provides scholarships, supports community engagements efforts, and provides specialized arts equipment and facility improvements. Their efforts expand opportunities and enhance the experience of students, instructors, and the community at-large. For more information about MAC or MACA, please call 503.823.2787 or visit www.multnomahartscenter.org.
events.title: A Good Universe Next Door

events.summary: Curated by Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK School and Lisa Jarrett Drawing from the Museum’s collection, this exhibition is co-curated by Lisa Jarrett, an artist, educator, and curator, and the Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK Elementary— a group of 4th and 5th grade curators from KSMoCA. Working from a conversation with notable curators Dr. Lowery Stokes Sims and Dr. Leslie King Hammond, the exhibition engages PAM’s collection in new dialogues shaped by emerging curatorial voices and multigenerational knowledge. From theme and concept development, through work selection, and installation, this community curators project highlights the collaborative nature of curatorial practice and museum work. Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK School \(HTC\) is a KSMoCA project. Students participate directly in shaping exhibitions, positioning them as contributors to the museum, and engaging them as researchers, writers, planners, and curators. Through workshops and field trips, students collaborate with artists, visiting curators, and mentors from Portland State University’s College of the Arts. They research how exhibitions are developed, how artworks are interpreted, and how institutional decisions shape public understanding. Expanded curatorial practice includes visual art, writing, performance, research, publishing, and social practice. Co-founded by Lisa Jarrett and Harrell Fletcher, the project began in 2018 at Harriet Tubman Middle School and continues in its current iteration at Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Elementary School.
events.title: Harriet Tubman Center Museum

events.summary: Inspired by Katherine Ace’s 9 Portraits as the foundational starting point for the exhibition, Nine Women Artists will feature the work of the artists shown in Ace’s portrait painting. All mature artists in their careers and with a significant presence in the Northwest, their work reveals a diverse expression of artistic styles from representation to abstraction. There are rich details in the painting. Most notably on the left hangs Henri Fantin-Latour’s A Studio at Les Batignolles, 1870 \(Musée d’Orsay\). In this painting is a formal gathering of male artists. In response to this painting, Katherine asked her subjects to dress in their studio/work clothes as counterpoint, all marked in their characteristic poses. Other Portland women artists are recognized here through their paintings—a small Sally Haley still life hangs in the background, as well as an Amanda Snyder painting behind Phyllis Yes. And to the far right, we have a glimpse of Lucinda Parker’s very large work. Postcards and newspapers scattered on the floor are the exhibition announcements and reviews highlighting the artists’ works. An epic portrait featuring nine women artists of the Northwest, Ace responded to the lack of self-portraits by women artists in history. From left, the artists are: Laura Ross-Paul, Katherine’s self-portrait seated with phone, Mary Josephson, Judy Cooke, Phyllis Yes, Sharon Bronzan, Shu-Ju Wang, Lucinda Parker, and Sherrie Wolf. All are women artists who have made long careers in Portland. As Ace notes about these women, “They have tenacity, have lived through sexist decades, told they couldn’t really be artists—only fit for sleeping with the professor, expected to subvert themselves to male artist machismo.”
events.title: Nine Women Artists

events.summary: Chefas Projects is pleased to present Galvanized, the first solo exhibition at the gallery by Portland artist Bobby Adams. On view September 18 through October 17, the exhibition brings together seven new gradient paintings that extend Adams’s ongoing investigation into color, movement, precision, and reduction. Working with hard edges and meticulously calibrated color transitions, Adams constructs paintings that appear at once exacting and elusive. Color becomes both subject and structure: gradients shift across the surface with a measured sense of movement, while simplified compositions heighten the perceptual effects of scale, saturation, and transition. The paintings inhabit a productive space between the mechanical and the handmade, where precision does not eliminate the presence of the artist but makes it more apparent. Adams’s approach is informed by a background outside of traditional art-making. Before turning to painting in 2017, he worked in product development and ran a clothing line for eight years. That experience with materials, systems, color, and visual identity remains embedded in his practice. His paintings share an affinity with the economy and immediacy of graphic design while resisting its fixedness; seemingly simple arrangements become dynamic through subtle shifts in color and proportion. The title Galvanized gestures toward a central tension within the work: the desire to achieve a polished, controlled image alongside the inevitable irregularities of its making. Adams’s paintings are rigorously constructed, but they are not anonymous. Their surfaces hold the evidence of decisions, adjustments, and the physical act of painting. Running through the exhibition is Adams’s longstanding relationship to NASCAR, a significant influence on his upbringing and visual sensibility. The sport’s saturated palettes, speed, spectacle, and graphic intensity provide an unexpected point of departure for paintings that are otherwise characterized by restraint. In California Poppy, this connection is particularly pronounced. Its color relationships carry the visual charge of racing culture while being distilled through Adams’s pared-down formal language. The result is a body of work in which speed is suggested rather than depicted, and where movement emerges from the most economical means. Adams takes visual cues associated with motion, competition, and spectacle and subjects them to the slower, more deliberate logic of abstraction. Galvanized marks an important step in Adams’s relationship with the gallery, following his inclusion in multiple group exhibitions and establishing a sustained presentation of his practice through a focused body of new work.
events.title: BOBBY ADAMS | GALVANIZED

events.summary: Chefas Projects is pleased to present Mercurial, a new solo exhibition by sculptural artist Dan Lam, on view September 18 through October 17, 2026. Bringing together more than twenty new works, the exhibition introduces a heightened metallic sensibility to Lam’s singular sculptural language, with surfaces that suggest chrome, liquid metal, and something less readily identifiable-objects caught somewhere between matter and mutation. Known for sculptures that occupy an uncanny space between the organic and the artificial, Lam approaches form as something fluid, seductive, and alive. In Mercurial, this sensibility takes on a distinctly reflective character. Metallic hues course across the surfaces of the works, emphasizing their bulbous contours, dripping edges, and seemingly unstable forms. Chrome-like finishes catch and distort their surroundings, allowing the sculptures to shift with changes in light, perspective, and proximity. The works appear to ooze, pool, drip, and swell. Their surfaces suggest viscosity while their forms remain resolutely sculptural, creating an intriguing contradiction between solidity and liquidity. They seem less like objects that have been made than organisms in the midst of becoming - alien, tactile, and strangely familiar. This tension is fundamental to Lam’s practice. Her sculptures consistently operate between opposing states: attraction and repulsion, organic and inanimate, soft and hard, seriousness and play. Rather than resolving these contradictions, Lam uses them as points of departure. The resulting forms possess an uncanny immediacy, inviting viewers to move closer even as their unfamiliarity introduces a note of hesitation. In Mercurial, the reflective surfaces intensify this exchange between object and viewer. The sculptures absorb fragments of their environments and return them altered, making the surrounding space part of the work. What initially reads as an autonomous object becomes something more relational-a form that changes depending on where it is encountered and how it is seen. Despite their otherworldly appearance, Lam’s sculptures remain remarkably approachable. Playfulness is central to their charge. The works resist the distance sometimes associated with contemporary sculpture, instead engaging the viewer through color, surface, scale, and a visceral sense of recognition. They are strange without being alienating; experimental without abandoning the pleasures of looking. The title Mercurial evokes both the mutable nature of the works and their affinity with mercury: a substance defined by its fluidity, reflectivity, and ability to transform its appearance in relation to its surroundings. Here, Lam translates those qualities into sculptural form. Her objects appear perpetually in motion, suspended between states, as though their final form has not yet been decided. Across more than twenty new sculptures, Mercurial expands Lam’s investigation of the space between the familiar and the unknown. The works activate the imagination through an intuitive visual language - one based not on representation but on sensation. Their exaggerated forms, seductive surfaces, and ambiguous materiality encourage viewers to project, imagine, and participate. In Lam’s hands, sculpture becomes less a fixed thing than an encounter: part organism, part object, part fantasy. Mercurial embraces that instability, presenting a body of work that is at once polished and unruly, seductive and strange, playful and profound.
events.title: DAN LAM | MERCURIAL

events.summary: Fridays in October 2026 | 2:00-4:00 PM | Free with admission or membership Summary Artist Bio Admission Parking Experience Overview As part of the Lion Reborn exhibition, Portland artist Joshua Sin invites visitors into his process every Friday in October from 2:00 to 4:00 PM. Watch as he builds a traditional Chinese lion head from scratch, right inside the garden. The same craft behind the suspended lion presiding overhead in the Scholar’s Study, brought to life before your eyes. Drawing on the intangible cultural heritage of Chinese lion dance craft, a tradition currently nominated for UNESCO recognition, Sin demonstrates the ancestral techniques of bending and weaving bamboo and rattan, layering it with reclaimed and festive materials by hand. Don’t miss this rare and intimate encounter with a living cultural tradition! All ages welcome. About the Artist Joshua Sin Joshua Sin is a Toronto-born, Portland-based sculptor and installation artist. A former world champion gymnast, he brings a lifelong discipline of repetition and precision to his work. After years in corporate design, including Nike’s retail concept stores in Tokyo, Seoul, and Berlin, Sin left the industry to pursue art independently. A residency with GLEAN and Recology, working inside Portland’s Northwest Transfer Station, reshaped his understanding of material. His ongoing Descendant Series, rooted in a centuries-old family ancestral book, reconstructs erased histories through reclaimed textiles. His work has been exhibited at the Jordan Schnitzer Museum of Art and the Portland Chinatown Museum. Their performances and installations integrate electrical signals and human presence, weaving dense networks of causality to form audiovisual environments that babble with a life-like current. events.summary: We Built You a Garden is the third installment of Metro’s Community Voices project, a multimedia storytelling initiative that invites residents of Metro Affordable Housing Bond-funded communities to explore the meaning of home through photography, writing and collective reflection. Hosted through a summer workshop series at the Strong Empowerment Village in partnership with artists Gwen Hoeffgen and Domenic Toliver, the project centers the experiences of residents with ties to North and Northeast Portland. Through weekly workshops and the use of film photography and creative writing, participants documented places, people and memories that shape their understanding of home, legacy and belonging. Their work considers displacement, resilience and community history, creating a powerful collection of stories that honor the past while imagining what can continue to grow. Ultimately, We Built You a Garden asks what’s been inherited, what’s been built, and what we want to leave growing for the next generation. It speaks to the ongoing impact of displacement in Portland for the Black community, but it also affirms what it took — and continues to take — to nourish, tend and build home. Exhibition and events: Free admission Oct. 9, 5:30pm to 8pm: We Built You a Garden | Exhibition Opening at The BLACK Gallery Join us for the opening of We Built You a Garden, with remarks and refreshments as well as free copies of the project’s publication. Open to public with remarks from Metro, artists, and Don’t Shoot PDX . Oct. 23, 6pm to 8pm: We Built You a Garden | Community Conversation at The BLACK Gallery A conversation about the past, present, and future of Portland through the experiences of the people who live, work, organize, and build here. Artists, activists, community members, youth and Metro come together to consider what we have inherited, what we have built, what is changing, and what we want to leave growing for the next generation. The BLACK Gallery will be open to the public on the following Sundays from 1pm to 4pm during the exhibition’s display: Oct. 11, Oct. 18, Oct. 25 and Nov. 1.
events.title: We Built You a Garden

events.summary: For this Culinary Cut of Coppola Movie Night, join us for an intimate screening of Francis Ford Coppola’s Bram Stoker’s Dracula, accompanied by a multi-course menu served in sync with the film. Rich, dramatic and just a little macabre, the menu takes its cues from the world on screen, with crimson ingredients, darker flavors and unexpected pairings woven throughout the evening. As the story unfolds, so does the dinner, with each course timed to specific moments in the film for an immersive experience created specifically for Dracula. Coppola’s 1992 adaptation of Bram Stoker’s gothic classic is known for its striking practical effects, elaborate costumes, saturated color and theatrical style. It’s exactly the kind of film that calls for something more than popcorn. events.summary: A Uniquely PDX STORYTELLING EXPERIENCE 𝐒𝐚𝐯𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐞 — October 9, 2026, RaeLoft, PDX ✨ 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐦𝐮𝐧𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐂𝐞𝐥𝐞𝐛𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧! Portland and Pacific Northwest friends: I hope you’ll join me for a very special evening of photography, storytelling, history, music and dance honoring Portland's performance culture "𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐞𝐬" and the forthcoming book 𝐒𝐮𝐛𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐚 & 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐂𝐮𝐥𝐭 𝐨𝐟 𝐀𝐩𝐡𝐫𝐨𝐝𝐢𝐭𝐞; 50 portraits and 13 interviews. This project grew out of my fascination with the 𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐨𝐟 𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐨𝐧𝐚 and the tension and balance between our creative muses as artists and the practicalities of paying the rent and feeding our families. The book is a portrait of a city known for its creative, rebellious and iconoclastic spirit. The subjects of these collaborative photographs and interviews will be at 𝐑𝐚𝐞 𝐋𝐨𝐟𝐭 (𝟐𝟐𝟐𝟐 𝐍𝐄 𝐎𝐫𝐞𝐠𝐨𝐧 𝐒𝐭𝐫𝐞𝐞𝐭) on 𝐎𝐜𝐭𝐨𝐛𝐞𝐫 𝟗, 𝟔–𝟏𝟎 𝐏𝐌, to tell their stories, perform and show their inner selves in full regalia. We’ll have bubbly, wine, food, music, dance, photography and plenty of visual spectacle, along with local vendors representing the products, businesses and services that make Portland so inventive and independent. We’ll also be joined by a historian who will explore the history of performance in Portland and the Pacific Northwest — including the cultural forces that helped give Portland its reputation for having the most strip clubs per capita and being known as the whitest city in America — connecting the artists and communities represented in Subrosa to the broader history of performance, vice, nightlife and creative expression in the region. This is a celebration of and 𝐠𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤 𝐭𝐨 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐬 who gave their time and stories to make the project possible, and of the remarkable creative community that helped bring the project and book to life. Save the date and share this with your Portland and Pacific Northwest friends. More details and tickets coming soon. Event 𝐋𝐢𝐦𝐢𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝟗𝟎 𝐬𝐞𝐚𝐭𝐬. 21+ TICKETS: https://www.subrosapdx.net/event-tickets-sponsorship \\Event ticket includes drinks, dinner, dessert, live entertainment, comedic performances, live auction, silent auction, and wall of wine. For the past seven years, photographer Jason Langer has documented Portland's unique EXOTIC DANCE, BURLESQUE, CIRCUS AND DRAG culture through portraiture and oral history, creating an intimate record of the performers whose lives and stories have helped shape the city's identity. Subrosa & the Cult of Aphrodite is both an art book and a cultural document, exploring themes of performance, labor, sexual identity, agency, and community. This event raises support for the publication and distribution of the book, helping preserve an important chapter of Oregon's cultural history and bring these stories to a wider audience.

events.summary: More than 15 years into its life as a Portland band, The Cabin Project returns October 9 with its seventh album, The Wonder, and an album release show that evening at Show Bar at Revolution Hall with Gillian Frances. On The Wonder, The Cabin Project draws on more than fifteen years of musical interplay while pushing its long-honed sound into wilder terrain. Rooted in the forests of the Pacific Northwest, the record moves through rupture and recovery toward renewal, tracing the gradual reemergence of our instinctive, wild and rooted selves. This movement takes shape in layered choral harmonies, inventive rhythms, atmospheric woodwinds, melodic bass and intricate guitar lines. Zanny Geffel’s restless drumming and percussion anchor arrangements shaped by Kelly Clifton’s bass and Mieke Bruggeman’s woodwinds, with Adam Sweeney—the original guitarist who helped propel the band from its folk beginnings toward rock—back in the lineup. This album dances between bare intimacy and collective orchestral force. It’s The Cabin Project at its most adventurous and texturally rich. The Cabin Project began in Portland in 2009 as founder Katie Sawicki moved from solo work toward a more collaborative practice. That commitment to collaboration extends well beyond the band: Sawicki is also an illustrator and strategic planner whose work with artists, justice workers and movement-building organizations spans visual art, organizational strategy, and racial and social justice. The same ethos of co-creation runs through The Cabin Project, a queer, women and nonbinary collective whose long musical relationships shape The Wonder from the inside out. Restless, visceral and tenacious, The Wonder - an album born of difficult years - resists easy resolution, turning rupture and recovery into songs that build, fracture and surge toward something larger. THE CABIN PROJECT — *THE WONDER* ALBUM RELEASE With Gillian Frances Friday, October 9, 2026 Show Bar at Revolution Hall Doors 7 pm | Music 8 pm | $15 | 21+ www.thecabinproject.com

events.summary: Jesse Preis debuts The Raven, a chamber opera composed for three voices and chamber ensemble from Edgar Allan Poe’s poem of the same name, directed by Melory Mirashrafi. In this opera, the narrator (split into two characters to capture the perspective of the Past and the Current at two different stages in life) deals with the loss of a loved one. These complicated, painful, and even terrifying emotions become personified through the character of the Raven. This work is composed with no specific voice types tied to the characters - anyone able to sing the part can and should sing them. This is a groundbreaking composing technique that unties the binds of gendered characters and allows vocalists to portray a character of any gender that is authentic to them and suits their voice. Preis seeks to expand our understanding of vocal writing to go beyond the gendered conventions of soprano, mezzo-soprano, tenor, and bass-baritone, and posits a world where characters are simply written and performed by a wide variety of voices.
events.title: The Raven

events.summary: Written in 1936, this light-hearted comedy has relevance for today in addressing the main theme of finding one’s own way in today’s complex society, while lightly viewing such topics as distrust of government, domestic terrorism and fear of foreign conflicts. “Grandpa” Vanderhof (Robert Lovitz) once worked in the competitive business world. One day, he realized he was unhappy, so he stopped working. Since then, he spends his days catching and raising snakes, watching graduation ceremonies, visiting old friends, and doing whatever else he wants. His daughter Penny (Marilyn Stacey) writes plays simply because a few years ago a typewriter was delivered to the house by accident. His son-in-law Paul Sycamore (Todd Hermanson) spends hours in the basement making illegal fireworks and playing with erector sets. His granddaughter Essie (Bonnie Auguston) sells candy and has been clumsily attempting ballet for over eight years. His grandson-in-law Ed Carmichael (Aiden Brown) plays the xylophone (or tries to) and accidentally distributes Marxist propaganda. Joining this free-for-all are Rheba (Caren Graham), the household cook; her unemployed boyfriend, Donald (Shaun Hennessy); Essie’s opinionated Russian ballet instructor, Mr. Kolenkhov (Mark Schwahn); Olga (Trisha Todd), a Russian Grand Duchess; Gay Wellington (Adrienne Southard), a heavy-drinking actress; Wilbur C. Henderson (Douglas Hout), a forlorn IRS employee; and Mr. De Pinna (Danny Bruno), a deliveryman who arrived 8 years ago and decided to stay. He now helps with the fireworks and dresses in Roman togas to pose for Penny’s portraits. All is somewhat calm until three men from the government (Christopher Sparks, Dan Weiss, and Erik James) visit to investigate Ed’s flyers. In this crazy mix of characters, there is also Alice (Taylor Jean Grady), Penny and Paul’s other daughter and, apparently, the only “normal” family member. She met Tony Kirby (Noah Matthew Rich) at his dad’s Wall Street investment firm, and they’ve fallen in love. Culture shock and fireworks fly when Mr. Kirby (Jeremy Southard) and Mrs. Kirby (Wendy Martel) come to visit. But the message is clear: “Life’s pretty simple if you just relax,” as Grandpa puts it. You Can’t Take It With You is directed by Don Alder. Set design is by Chris Whitten, lighting design is by Demetri Pavlatos, costume design is by Janelle Sutton, prop design is by Allen R. Phillips, the stage manager is Alex Salem, the assistant stage manager is Nat Weinham, and the producer is Steve Knox.

events.summary: Adapted from Agatha Christie’s classic mystery, this immersive production brings the psychological tension of the classic tale into immediate, breath-held proximity. Our story takes place inside a remote seaside mansion after a violent storm strands ten guests and their hosts. When an eerie accusation recorded on a gramophone accuses each of them of wrongdoing, the guests confront secrets, guilt, and suspicion. Trapped by weather and circumstance, alliances form and fracture… old grievances surface, and rationality gives way to intense fear as each new death raises the stakes. At ETP’s production, you’ll find yourself sitting with the characters within the house itself, among the bedrooms, the dining room, and narrow passages. Experience the shifting power dynamics and mounting claustrophobia as if you were part of the action. Hear whispered confrontations up close, overhear private confessions, and feel the silence before the next crisis. Though the environment surrounds you, the audience is strictly non-participatory — as a silent witness, a “fly on the wall,” you will never be directly addressed by the characters, nor asked to participate. What to expect in performance: \- Tension-driven mystery with tightly controlled pacing and sudden shocks. \- Strong emphasis on atmosphere: storm sound design, flickering lantern and candlelight, thunder, and selective blackout moments. \- Intense emotional scenes: accusations, breakdowns, moral reckonings, and desperate attempts to find the culprit. \- Minimalist, realistic set dressing that transforms the performance space into a lived-in island mansion, with audience seating integrated into set locations (chairs, benches, window alcoves). \- No audience interaction; observers remain silent and stationary throughout each performance. Content warnings: Multiple onstage deaths and depictions of violence (staged, non-graphic). Mature themes and dialogue — recommended for ages 13+ About Experience Theatre Project: Experience Theatre Project is an innovative, immersive theater company based in Aloha, Oregon. Unlike traditional theaters with rows of seats and a proscenium stage, ETP crafts imaginative and fully surrounding narratives, drawing inspiration from both original and classic stories. Our specialty lies in presenting these tales in an unconventional, unexpected fashion, surrounding audiences in the world of the play, similar to a haunted house or a Disney experience. Limiting audiences to sixty or fewer ensures an intimate and memorable experience. Ticket link: www.experiencetheatreproject.org
events.title: ETP Presents Agatha Christie's And Then There Were None

events.summary: MSHR is an art collective that collaboratively builds and explores sculptural electronic systems. Their performances and installations integrate electrical signals and human presence, weaving dense networks of causality to form audiovisual environments that babble with a life-like current. They explore intuitive and technical gradients between sonic and sculptural forms, using analog circuitry and open-source software to sculpt mutually resonant hyperobjects. MSHR was founded by Brenna Murphy and Birch Cooper in 2011 in Portland, Oregon, as an offshoot from the collective Oregon Painting Society. The name MSHR is a modular acronym designed to hold varied ideas over time. It can be pronounced as an acronym or like one who meshes. website: www.MSHR.info The Tenses is a duo comprised of Ju Suk Reet Meate and Jackie Oblivia, core members of legendary group Smegma, founded in 1973 and veterans of the infamous sonic arts collective known as The Los Angeles Free Music Society. The duo was founded in 2008, using musical concepts developed over 40 years of organized and spontaneous sound making, with a focus on “live performance” in which the room has a major effect on the unfolding sounds. Instrumentation includes Record Player, Lap Steel Guitar, Pocket Trumpet , Electronics, Toys, etc. The name “The Tenses” is a title of a story in the book “The Dream World of Dion McGregor” from 1964. It is a unique book in that the stories are not “written”, but transcribed from stories told while asleep! website: https://smegmamusic.com/site/?cat=3 As ‘The Garbage Man’, Liz Harris of Grouper DJ’s odd tunes and scavenged mash-ups of obscure pop, classical, noise, and field recording on vinyl and cassette.

events.summary: Satin Jackets, the brainchild of German music producer Tim Bernhardt, has been a shining star in the music scene since its inception in 2012. Drawing inspiration from the polished productions of icons like Chic and studio genius Trevor Horn, Tim embarked on a mission to bring back the glamour and sheen of the modern disco era. “It always sounded like the musical equivalent of a fashion magazine’s cover,” Tim elaborates. The result of his creative pursuit was “You Make Me Feel Good,” a sublimely laidback slice of Balearic House that served as Satin Jackets’ introduction to the world. Released on the renowned Belgian label Eskimo Recordings, this single swiftly established Tim as a prominent figure in the thriving nu-disco scene, even though the face behind Satin Jackets remained somewhat of a mystery. Nevertheless, his warm sound resonated with music lovers worldwide. Over a decade has passed since the inception of Satin Jackets, and the project shows no signs of slowing down. With three outstanding albums in its discography, Satin Jackets continues to evolve, captivating and enchanting audiences across the globe. Collaborating with a stellar lineup of artists, including Panama, Tensnake, and Booka Shade, Satin Jackets has crafted a musical journey that pays homage to its disco roots while pushing the boundaries of modern sound. In the summer of 2025, the fourth album Cruise Control was released on his own label, marking another milestone in the project’s evolution. Since 2023, Tim has been releasing his music on his own label, Golden Hour Recordings, in a quest to refine his art and elevate it to the next level. He can now be found effortlessly moving between the vibrant scenes of clubs and rooftops around the world as well as Berlin, the heart of Germany’s music scene. With more than a decade of innovative tunes and musical adventures, the journey of Satin Jackets is as vibrant and compelling as the music itself.
events.title: Satin Jackets

His reputation has invited him opportunities to collaborate with Grammy Award-winning artists such as Tommy Emmanuel, with whom he recorded the duet record ‘Accomplice Vol. 3’, and the Grammy-nominated metal band Periphery, with whom Mike joined on their 2024 double single release. Mike is featured on multiple Justin Hayward live releases including Spirits…Live, which debuted at \#2 on the US Billboard chart. Dawes also has a strong reputation as an educator, acting as a columnist for Guitar World and Acoustic Guitar magazines as well as teaching guitar masterclasses all over the world, creating apps, publishing degree-level literature, appearing as a TV judge on Sky TV’s ‘Guitar Star’, and more. Recently he contributed electric guitars to Mentrix and Gareth Croker’s stunning soundtrack to Ubisoft’s Prince of Persia: The Lost Crown, with other session work featured on TV shows such as AMC’s Better Call Saul. Mike’s passion, however, is performing. Having shared the stage with acts as diverse as Tommy Emmanuel, Christopher Cross, Periphery, The Aristocrats, Justin Hayward and the Athens State Orchestra in 2023 alone. His third studio album, Galactic Acid, is anticipated for release in August 2024. “HE SLAPS, TAPS, AND CARESSES HIS WAY TO BRILLIANCE” Guitar World Magazine “DAWES IS JAW DROPPING” Guitar Player Magazine “THE ACOUSTIC TAPPING TITAN” Total Guitar Magazine/ MusicRadar “F\#@CKING AWESOME” James Hetfield \(Metallica\)

events.summary: The Multnomah Arts Center (MAC) presents A Good Universe Next Door – A redacted past, a precarious present, and an uncertain future, a group exhibition curated by Celeste Noche and Melanie Stevens. On view in the Front & Center Galleries from September 18 through October 17, 2026, the exhibition features new work by four regional artists: Amber Capwell, Ebony Frison, Maryanna Hollomon, and Orlando Almanza. An opening reception will be held Saturday, September 19, from 1–3 p.m., and an artist talk will take place Saturday, October 10 at 2 p.m. Stevens and Noche invited the artists to consider how utopia and dystopia manifest in their lives, and how they interpret these experiences. Through sculpture, photography, printmaking, and painting, the artists offer visions of futures shaped by remembrance, resistance, solidarity, creativity, and care. Ebony Frison approaches utopia and dystopia as “conditions that coexist within the same historical moment.” Working with archival research, printmaking, photography, and artist books, Frison examines how Black histories persist despite erasure, describing utopia as “a practice of rememory—an active engagement with ancestral knowledge, community care, and historical reclamation.” Maryanna Hollomon highlights the aftermath of war for children and the global systems that produce displacement. “A utopia cannot be achieved without working in solidarity with those most oppressed,” she writes. Her work asks viewers to consider militarism’s impact and to imagine new forms of resistance and collective care. Amber Capwell creates sculptural works that envision utopian possibilities through Tarot readings for endangered Pacific Northwest flora and fauna. “These sculptures exist as a reminder to care,” they write. Their work incorporates queer and trans identities as part of an ecological futurism that demands “a utopia existing where we are allowed to live and thrive.” Orlando Almanza imagines futures built on safety, connection, and community. “I dream of a place where my people can have picnics next to the river, to rest, to laugh… and the grandmothers can enjoy their old age, sitting in their rocking chairs on their front porch,” he writes. “Sueño con el día que pueda ver a mi familia reunida, en la tierra que nos vio nacer” (I dream that one day my family can be reunited, in the land that birthed us). The Multnomah Arts Center is located at 7688 SW Capitol Hwy, Portland, OR, 97219. It is open Monday – Thursday 9 a.m. to 9:30 p.m., and Friday – Saturday 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Additional Information: The Multnomah Arts Center is a part of Portland Parks & Recreation. MAC offers programs in a wide range of visual, music, movement, theater, and literary arts at an affordable cost to people of all ages. In addition to this vibrant arts education program, MAC runs a community-based visual arts exhibition program, which includes the MAC Front & Center Galleries. MAC also hosts theatre, music and dance performances, and other special events. The Multnomah Arts Center Association (MACA) is an all-volunteer, 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization that exists to support equity and access to arts education at MAC. MACA provides scholarships, supports community engagements efforts, and provides specialized arts equipment and facility improvements. Their efforts expand opportunities and enhance the experience of students, instructors, and the community at-large. For more information about MAC or MACA, please call 503.823.2787 or visit www.multnomahartscenter.org.
events.title: A Good Universe Next Door

events.summary: Curated by Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK School and Lisa Jarrett Drawing from the Museum’s collection, this exhibition is co-curated by Lisa Jarrett, an artist, educator, and curator, and the Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK Elementary— a group of 4th and 5th grade curators from KSMoCA. Working from a conversation with notable curators Dr. Lowery Stokes Sims and Dr. Leslie King Hammond, the exhibition engages PAM’s collection in new dialogues shaped by emerging curatorial voices and multigenerational knowledge. From theme and concept development, through work selection, and installation, this community curators project highlights the collaborative nature of curatorial practice and museum work. Harriet Tubman Center for Expanded Curatorial Practice at MLK School \(HTC\) is a KSMoCA project. Students participate directly in shaping exhibitions, positioning them as contributors to the museum, and engaging them as researchers, writers, planners, and curators. Through workshops and field trips, students collaborate with artists, visiting curators, and mentors from Portland State University’s College of the Arts. They research how exhibitions are developed, how artworks are interpreted, and how institutional decisions shape public understanding. Expanded curatorial practice includes visual art, writing, performance, research, publishing, and social practice. Co-founded by Lisa Jarrett and Harrell Fletcher, the project began in 2018 at Harriet Tubman Middle School and continues in its current iteration at Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Elementary School.
events.title: Harriet Tubman Center Museum

events.summary: Inspired by Katherine Ace’s 9 Portraits as the foundational starting point for the exhibition, Nine Women Artists will feature the work of the artists shown in Ace’s portrait painting. All mature artists in their careers and with a significant presence in the Northwest, their work reveals a diverse expression of artistic styles from representation to abstraction. There are rich details in the painting. Most notably on the left hangs Henri Fantin-Latour’s A Studio at Les Batignolles, 1870 \(Musée d’Orsay\). In this painting is a formal gathering of male artists. In response to this painting, Katherine asked her subjects to dress in their studio/work clothes as counterpoint, all marked in their characteristic poses. Other Portland women artists are recognized here through their paintings—a small Sally Haley still life hangs in the background, as well as an Amanda Snyder painting behind Phyllis Yes. And to the far right, we have a glimpse of Lucinda Parker’s very large work. Postcards and newspapers scattered on the floor are the exhibition announcements and reviews highlighting the artists’ works. An epic portrait featuring nine women artists of the Northwest, Ace responded to the lack of self-portraits by women artists in history. From left, the artists are: Laura Ross-Paul, Katherine’s self-portrait seated with phone, Mary Josephson, Judy Cooke, Phyllis Yes, Sharon Bronzan, Shu-Ju Wang, Lucinda Parker, and Sherrie Wolf. All are women artists who have made long careers in Portland. As Ace notes about these women, “They have tenacity, have lived through sexist decades, told they couldn’t really be artists—only fit for sleeping with the professor, expected to subvert themselves to male artist machismo.”
events.title: Nine Women Artists

It plays an essential role in both festive celebrations and everyday life. We warmly invite you to join this Chinese cooking demonstration led by culinary expert Anna. She will demonstrate how to use locally sourced ingredients to create simple, authentic homestyle dishes that capture the true flavors of home. Get Admission Featured at the event: The Asian Food Pantry \(AFP\) Cookbook — a culturally inspired collection of recipes using ingredients commonly distributed through the pantry over the past six years. Cookbooks will be available for purchase, with all proceeds supporting the Asian Food Pantry and its work serving low-income Asian seniors in our community. Meet the Demonstrator: Anna Xu is a passionate baker and home cook, known for her expertise in traditional Shanghainese cuisine as well as Western pastries. She is the author of The Taste of Home, Where The Heart Belongs 家的味道，心的归属, a bi-lingual cookbook that celebrates the emotional connections we build through food and a fundraising initiative that supports the pantry’s mission. Anna also leads the Asian Food Pantry program at the Community for Positive Aging \(Hollywood Senior Center\), where she supports low-income Asian seniors by providing culturally familiar foods and fostering community connection. A longtime volunteer at Lan Su Chinese Garden, Anna is deeply committed to promoting and preserving Chinese culture through her work and community engagement. events.summary: More than 40 leading local architecture firms present the best designs they hoped to build but that didn’t come to pass. Projects will include Allied Works’ elegant proposal commissioned by the New York Metropolitan Museum for its Modern and Contemporary Art Wing, West of West’s concept studies for infill housing in Los Angeles and Portland, Henneberry Eddy’s adaptive reuse of the recently destroyed Centennial Mills, and many more. In addition, the exhibition offers visions from Portland’s past, from Edward Bennett’s 1932 plan to reenvision Portland in the City Beautiful movement to Skidmore Owings Merrill’s “Delta Dome,” a 40,000-seat stadium in Delta Park, to GGN’s radical re-envisioning of Mt Tabor Park. It's a survey of Portland's past ambitions and its current array of design talent!
events.title: Unseen Portland Architecture: the best of Portland design. Never built

events.summary: Stringing Beads / Ensartar Cuentas brings together the work of Orquidia Violeta, Mariela Finvarb, Beatriz Bellorín, and Marisol Valencia in an exhibition that grew from the relationships formed during and after the 2024 Stelo Summer Invitational Residency. Expanded through a year of virtual gatherings, the exhibition reflects on how artistic dialogue continues to shape creative practice beyond the residency itself. Through photography, video, textiles, ceramics, painting, and installation, the artists explore migration, identity, memory, grief, ecology, ancestral knowledge, and care. Like beads threaded together, each work retains its individuality while contributing to a larger conversation about belonging, transformation, and the enduring connections forged through shared experience. Special featured artist: amoqiix-araceli
events.title: Ensartar Cuentas

events.summary: Chefas Projects is pleased to present Mercurial, a new solo exhibition by sculptural artist Dan Lam, on view September 18 through October 17, 2026. Bringing together more than twenty new works, the exhibition introduces a heightened metallic sensibility to Lam’s singular sculptural language, with surfaces that suggest chrome, liquid metal, and something less readily identifiable-objects caught somewhere between matter and mutation. Known for sculptures that occupy an uncanny space between the organic and the artificial, Lam approaches form as something fluid, seductive, and alive. In Mercurial, this sensibility takes on a distinctly reflective character. Metallic hues course across the surfaces of the works, emphasizing their bulbous contours, dripping edges, and seemingly unstable forms. Chrome-like finishes catch and distort their surroundings, allowing the sculptures to shift with changes in light, perspective, and proximity. The works appear to ooze, pool, drip, and swell. Their surfaces suggest viscosity while their forms remain resolutely sculptural, creating an intriguing contradiction between solidity and liquidity. They seem less like objects that have been made than organisms in the midst of becoming - alien, tactile, and strangely familiar. This tension is fundamental to Lam’s practice. Her sculptures consistently operate between opposing states: attraction and repulsion, organic and inanimate, soft and hard, seriousness and play. Rather than resolving these contradictions, Lam uses them as points of departure. The resulting forms possess an uncanny immediacy, inviting viewers to move closer even as their unfamiliarity introduces a note of hesitation. In Mercurial, the reflective surfaces intensify this exchange between object and viewer. The sculptures absorb fragments of their environments and return them altered, making the surrounding space part of the work. What initially reads as an autonomous object becomes something more relational-a form that changes depending on where it is encountered and how it is seen. Despite their otherworldly appearance, Lam’s sculptures remain remarkably approachable. Playfulness is central to their charge. The works resist the distance sometimes associated with contemporary sculpture, instead engaging the viewer through color, surface, scale, and a visceral sense of recognition. They are strange without being alienating; experimental without abandoning the pleasures of looking. The title Mercurial evokes both the mutable nature of the works and their affinity with mercury: a substance defined by its fluidity, reflectivity, and ability to transform its appearance in relation to its surroundings. Here, Lam translates those qualities into sculptural form. Her objects appear perpetually in motion, suspended between states, as though their final form has not yet been decided. Across more than twenty new sculptures, Mercurial expands Lam’s investigation of the space between the familiar and the unknown. The works activate the imagination through an intuitive visual language - one based not on representation but on sensation. Their exaggerated forms, seductive surfaces, and ambiguous materiality encourage viewers to project, imagine, and participate. In Lam’s hands, sculpture becomes less a fixed thing than an encounter: part organism, part object, part fantasy. Mercurial embraces that instability, presenting a body of work that is at once polished and unruly, seductive and strange, playful and profound.
events.title: DAN LAM | MERCURIAL

events.summary: Chefas Projects is pleased to present Galvanized, the first solo exhibition at the gallery by Portland artist Bobby Adams. On view September 18 through October 17, the exhibition brings together seven new gradient paintings that extend Adams’s ongoing investigation into color, movement, precision, and reduction. Working with hard edges and meticulously calibrated color transitions, Adams constructs paintings that appear at once exacting and elusive. Color becomes both subject and structure: gradients shift across the surface with a measured sense of movement, while simplified compositions heighten the perceptual effects of scale, saturation, and transition. The paintings inhabit a productive space between the mechanical and the handmade, where precision does not eliminate the presence of the artist but makes it more apparent. Adams’s approach is informed by a background outside of traditional art-making. Before turning to painting in 2017, he worked in product development and ran a clothing line for eight years. That experience with materials, systems, color, and visual identity remains embedded in his practice. His paintings share an affinity with the economy and immediacy of graphic design while resisting its fixedness; seemingly simple arrangements become dynamic through subtle shifts in color and proportion. The title Galvanized gestures toward a central tension within the work: the desire to achieve a polished, controlled image alongside the inevitable irregularities of its making. Adams’s paintings are rigorously constructed, but they are not anonymous. Their surfaces hold the evidence of decisions, adjustments, and the physical act of painting. Running through the exhibition is Adams’s longstanding relationship to NASCAR, a significant influence on his upbringing and visual sensibility. The sport’s saturated palettes, speed, spectacle, and graphic intensity provide an unexpected point of departure for paintings that are otherwise characterized by restraint. In California Poppy, this connection is particularly pronounced. Its color relationships carry the visual charge of racing culture while being distilled through Adams’s pared-down formal language. The result is a body of work in which speed is suggested rather than depicted, and where movement emerges from the most economical means. Adams takes visual cues associated with motion, competition, and spectacle and subjects them to the slower, more deliberate logic of abstraction. Galvanized marks an important step in Adams’s relationship with the gallery, following his inclusion in multiple group exhibitions and establishing a sustained presentation of his practice through a focused body of new work.
events.title: BOBBY ADAMS | GALVANIZED

events.summary: Jesse Preis debuts The Raven, a chamber opera composed for three voices and chamber ensemble from Edgar Allan Poe’s poem of the same name, directed by Melory Mirashrafi. In this opera, the narrator (split into two characters to capture the perspective of the Past and the Current at two different stages in life) deals with the loss of a loved one. These complicated, painful, and even terrifying emotions become personified through the character of the Raven. This work is composed with no specific voice types tied to the characters - anyone able to sing the part can and should sing them. This is a groundbreaking composing technique that unties the binds of gendered characters and allows vocalists to portray a character of any gender that is authentic to them and suits their voice. Preis seeks to expand our understanding of vocal writing to go beyond the gendered conventions of soprano, mezzo-soprano, tenor, and bass-baritone, and posits a world where characters are simply written and performed by a wide variety of voices.
events.title: The Raven

In 2026, the band celebrates the 10 year anniversary of their breakthrough album Unfamiliar, the record that helped define a generation of emotionally charged pop-punk and introduced fans to songs that still hit just as hard today. From bedroom speakers to packed clubs around the world, Unfamiliar became more than just an album. It became a soundtrack for growing up, falling apart, and figuring yourself out along the way. To celebrate the milestone, the band will be performing Unfamiliar in full on a special anniversary co-headline tour alongside longtime scene favorites Every Avenue. Bringing together two bands whose songs helped shape the soundtrack of the late 2000s and 2010s emo and pop punk scene, the tour is designed as both a nostalgic celebration and a reminder of why these songs continue to resonate with fans years later. , "rdquo" -> Ten years ago we made Unfamiliar as a bunch of kids trying to process anxiety, heartbreak, growing pains, and everything in between," says vocalist Joey Fleming. , "rdquo" -> We never imagined those songs would still mean this much to people a decade later. Seeing fans scream these lyrics back to us after all this time is honestly surreal." While the anniversary tour celebrates the album that changed everything for the band, In Her Own Words aren't simply revisiting the past. Behind the scenes, the band has spent the last year working on a brand new full-length album, one they describe as their most ambitious and emotionally honest material to date. With new music expected in 2026, this tour marks both a celebration of where the band came from and the beginning of an entirely new chapter. Every Avenue Bio: Every Avenue is an American pop-punk band from Marysville, Michigan, formed in 2003. Before their temporary disbandment, the group consisted of David Ryan Strauchman (lead vocals, piano), Joshua Randall Withenshaw (lead guitar), Jimmie Deeghan (rhythm guitar, backing vocals), Matt Black (bass, backing vocals) and Dennis Wilson (drums, percussion). The band is signed to Fearless Records and released their debut album, Shh, Just Go with it in 2008. It was followed up by their second album, Picture Perfect, in 2009, which reached No. 136 on Billboard 200. In 2011, the band's latest and third album titled Bad Habits was released, and it peaked at No. 63 on Billboard 200, being the band's highest chart position and sold over 300,000 Records Worldwide.. Every Avenue has toured with bands such as Mayday Parade, All Time Low, The Maine on The Compromising of Integrity, Morality and Principles in Exchange for Money Tour, Boys Like Girls, and have appeared on the Vans Warped Tour. In 2023, David Strauchman announced , "rdquo" -> The Light In The Dark" Tour with support from rising pop-punk band Makeout, and emo-pioneer SayWeCanFly including co-headline dates with Sparks The Rescue.
